m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a notebook in Google Colab and connect it to a free runtime.
  • Run code cells and read the output that appears under each one.
  • Confirm that pandas, NumPy, and Matplotlib load, and draw a first chart.
  • Set up JupyterLab instead, if you'd rather work offline on your own computer.
  • Fix the four setup problems students hit most often.

Here is a complete analysis in about a dozen lines. It builds a year of daily temperatures, finds the hottest week, and draws the whole year as a chart. In a spreadsheet you would click through menus for ten minutes, and next year you would click through them again. In a notebook you write the steps once and rerun them on new data in a second.

You don't need to understand every line yet. By Module 3 you will. Right now the goal is a notebook where this code runs.

#What you need, and what you don't

This course uses Google Colab, a free notebook that runs in your browser. Your code runs on a computer in a Google data center, which already has pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, seaborn, and scikit-learn installed. You install nothing.

You need three things:

  1. A Google account. A personal account always works. School accounts work only if your school's administrator has switched Colab on, so if a school account shows an access message, try a personal one or ask your teacher.
  2. A current browser. Google says Colab is tested most on the latest Chrome, Firefox, and Safari. Edge works too.
  3. An internet connection. Because the code runs remotely, Colab stops working when you go offline. If that's a problem where you study, use JupyterLab (further down this page).

You don't need a GPU, a paid plan, or a powerful laptop. Every dataset in this course is small enough for the free tier.

#Make your first notebook, step by step

  1. Go to colab.research.google.com and click Sign in in the top right if you aren't signed in already.
  2. A window for opening notebooks appears. Click New notebook at the bottom of it. If the window doesn't appear, use File › New notebook in Drive.
  3. The notebook opens with a name like Untitled0.ipynb. Click that name at the top left and rename it ds-setup.ipynb. Colab saves it in a folder called Colab Notebooks in your Google Drive.
  4. Click inside the gray box. That box is a code cell. Type print("ready").
  5. Press Shift + Enter, or click the round play button at the left edge of the cell.

The first run takes a few seconds, because Colab has to start a machine for you. That machine is called the runtime. When it's ready, the top right shows small RAM and Disk bars, and ready appears under your cell. A small number in square brackets next to the cell, like [1], counts the order in which cells ran.

Windows

  • Shift + Enter: run the cell and move to the next one.
  • Ctrl + Enter: run the cell and stay on it.
  • Ctrl + M, then B: add a code cell below.
  • Ctrl + M, then M: turn the cell into a text (Markdown) cell.
  • Ctrl + S: save now. Colab also saves automatically as you work.

macOS

  • Shift + Return: run the cell and move to the next one.
  • ⌘ + Return: run the cell and stay on it.
  • ⌘ + M, then B: add a code cell below.
  • ⌘ + M, then M: turn the cell into a text (Markdown) cell.
  • ⌘ + S: save a checkpoint right away.

Chromebook

  • Shortcuts match Windows: Shift + Enter runs and moves on, Ctrl + Enter runs and stays.
  • Ctrl + M, then B adds a code cell below; Ctrl + M, then M makes a text cell.
  • Open Colab in a normal Chrome tab. Colab is the recommended path on a Chromebook, since installing JupyterLab needs the Linux development environment, which school Chromebooks often block.

For the full list, open Tools › Keyboard shortcuts.

JupyterLab is the open-source notebook that Colab grew out of. The notebooks are the same .ipynb files, and every lesson in this course runs in it. Choose it if you have your own computer and want to work offline. It takes about ten minutes to set up.

Chromebook

Use Colab. JupyterLab needs Linux apps, which you turn on under Settings › About ChromeOS › Developers › Linux development environment. Many school Chromebooks hide that option. If yours has it, follow the macOS steps inside the Linux terminal after running sudo apt install python3-venv.

Your browser opens a page whose address starts with http://localhost:8888. Click Python 3 (ipykernel) under Notebook in the Launcher to make a notebook. Leave the terminal window open while you work; closing it stops JupyterLab.

#When it doesn't work: the four usual problems

1. "Colab isn't available" or an access-denied page. This usually means a school account where Colab is switched off. Sign in with a personal Google account in a different browser profile, or use JupyterLab.

2. The cell shows a spinning circle and nothing happens. Look at the top right. If it still says Connecting, the runtime hasn't started yet; wait 30 seconds, then reload the page. If the page complains about a GPU, open Runtime › Change runtime type and choose CPU. This course never needs a GPU.

3. A cell fails with NameError. You ran a cell that uses a name before the cell that creates it. This is what happens if you run a cell that uses survey before any cell has defined it:

Read the last line of the error first: Python is saying survey doesn't exist in the runtime's memory. Run the earlier cells (Runtime › Run before runs everything above the current cell), then try again. You'll also see this after Colab disconnects an idle notebook, because a fresh runtime starts with empty memory.

4. JupyterLab says ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'. The library went into a different Python than the one your notebook uses. Run this in a notebook cell, which installs into the notebook's own Python, then restart the kernel with Kernel › Restart Kernel:

On a Mac, pip sometimes refuses with externally-managed-environment. That means you skipped the venv step; go back and create the environment.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You open your notebook the next morning and run only the chart cell. It fails with NameError: name 'pd' is not defined. Why?

  • Colab's libraries stay installed; what's gone is the memory of what you imported.

  • Idle notebooks get a fresh runtime with empty memory. Run the import cell (or Runtime › Run before) first.

  • One run is enough once the names it uses exist.

Show answer

B. Idle notebooks get a fresh runtime with empty memory. Run the import cell (or Runtime › Run before) first.

2Where does your Python code actually run when you use Colab?

  • The browser only shows the notebook; the work happens elsewhere.

  • That's why Colab works on a Chromebook and why it stops working offline.

  • Drive stores the notebook file, but Drive doesn't run code.

Show answer

B. That's why Colab works on a Chromebook and why it stops working offline.

Key takeaways

  • Colab is a free notebook in the browser; the code runs on a Google machine called the runtime, with the data libraries preinstalled.
  • Shift + Enter runs a cell. The [n] beside it shows the order cells ran in.
  • Notebooks save to the Colab Notebooks folder in your Drive.
  • JupyterLab runs the same .ipynb notebooks locally and offline.
  • NameError in a notebook usually means an earlier cell hasn't run in this runtime yet.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find your way around Colab: code cells, text cells, the Files panel, and the runtime.
  • Get a CSV from your computer into Colab two ways, and load it with pd.read_csv.
  • Draw a chart from the file and write a summary file back out.
  • Mount Google Drive so your data and results outlive the runtime.

You've downloaded a survey export called lunch_survey.csv, and it's sitting in your Downloads folder. You open Colab and type pd.read_csv("lunch_survey.csv"), and get FileNotFoundError. The file is right there on your laptop, but your code doesn't run on your laptop. It runs on the runtime, a separate machine that has never seen your Downloads folder.

That one fact explains most of this lesson. Three places are involved, and you need to know which one holds what:

The runtime is temporary. When it shuts down, everything on it goes too: variables, uploaded files, files your code wrote. Your notebook survives because it lives in Drive, but data has to be put somewhere safe on purpose.

#A quick tour of the Colab window

Open the ds-setup.ipynb notebook from the last lesson (or make a new one). Five parts of the window matter:

  • The cells in the middle. Gray code cells run Python. Text cells hold notes written in Markdown. The + Code and + Text buttons near the top add a new cell below the one you're on.
  • The left sidebar. The folder icon opens the Files panel, a view of the runtime's disk. The {x} icon opens Variables, which lists every name currently in memory with its type and value. The list icon at the top is a Table of contents built from your text-cell headings.
  • The Runtime menu. Run all cells, run everything above the current cell, interrupt a cell that's stuck, or restart with empty memory.
  • The RAM and Disk bars at the top right, which only appear while you're connected.
  • The File menu. Rename, save a copy, or download the notebook as .ipynb.

Double-click a text cell to edit it. A few lines of Markdown give your notebook a structure you'll thank yourself for later:

Press Shift + Enter and the text cell renders as a heading and formatted notes.

#Step 1: Get a CSV into the runtime

You have two ways to upload a file from your computer.

Option A, the Files panel. Click the folder icon in the left sidebar, then the upload button at the top of the panel (a page with an upward arrow). Pick your CSV. It appears in the list, inside the runtime's working folder, /content. Colab shows a reminder that uploaded files are deleted when the runtime ends; it means it.

Option B, from code. Run this in a cell. A Choose Files button appears under the cell:

Both options put the file in /content, which is the folder read_csv looks in when you give it a bare file name.

Don't have a CSV handy? This cell writes one into the runtime, so the rest of the lesson works for everyone. A CSV is plain text: a header line naming the columns, then one line per row, with commas between values.

Click the refresh button in the Files panel and lunch_survey.csv shows up, as if you had uploaded it.

#Step 2: Load it and look

survey.shape is (rows, columns): 18 responses, 5 columns. head() shows the first five rows, so you can see that the header became column names and the values landed in the right places. Those two lines are the first thing to run on any file you load. Module 2 covers the rest of the first-look checklist.

🧪 Try it yourself

Open the {x} Variables panel now. You'll see survey listed as a DataFrame with its shape. Run survey = 5 in a new cell and watch the entry change. Then rerun the read_csv cell to put it back.

#Step 3: Turn it into a chart

Which meal is most popular, and which is rated highest? Those are two different questions, so they get two different numbers:

Read the printed numbers before the chart. Pizza has the most fans by far, yet the Salad bar has the highest average rating, and that average comes from only three students. A single "most popular" answer would have hidden both facts.

#Step 4: Save results so they survive

Write the summary to a CSV in the runtime:

Reading the file straight back is a cheap way to check that what you saved is what you meant to save. To get it onto your laptop, find lunch_summary.csv in the Files panel, open its three-dot menu, and choose Download, or run files.download("lunch_summary.csv") after the files import above.

Downloading by hand gets old fast. The better habit is to keep your course data in Google Drive and let Colab read and write there directly. Mounting Drive makes it appear as a folder inside the runtime. Run this in Colab:

When drive.mount runs, Colab asks you to pick your Google account and allow access. Once it prints Mounted at /content/drive, your Drive is the folder /content/drive/MyDrive, and anything saved under it really is in Drive. Loading works the same way: pd.read_csv(f"{folder}/lunch_survey.csv"), once the file is in that folder.

Put your raw CSV files in MyDrive/ds-course once (drag them into drive.google.com), and every future notebook can load them with one line after mounting.

⚠️ Watch out

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'lunch_survey.csv' has three usual causes. The runtime restarted and deleted your upload, so upload it again or load it from Drive. The name is slightly different (lunch_survey (1).csv after a second download is common), so copy the exact name from the Files panel. Or the file is in Drive and you forgot the folder, so use the full /content/drive/MyDrive/... path. In the Files panel, a file's three-dot menu has Copy path, which avoids typos.

#Proof it works: a checklist

Your setup is done when you can tick all five:

  1. A notebook named ds-setup.ipynb exists in Colab Notebooks in your Drive.
  2. It has at least one text cell with a heading.
  3. It loads a CSV with pd.read_csv and prints its shape.
  4. It draws a chart under a cell.
  5. It writes a file into MyDrive/ds-course and that file shows up at drive.google.com.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You upload scores.csv through the Files panel, work for an hour, take a long break, and come back. pd.read_csv("scores.csv") now fails with FileNotFoundError. What happened?

  • Colab doesn't rename uploads; check the Files panel and you'll find it's gone, not renamed.

  • Uploads live on the temporary runtime. Keep data in Drive to avoid uploading it again.

  • You can read a file as many times as you like while it exists.

Show answer

B. Uploads live on the temporary runtime. Keep data in Drive to avoid uploading it again.

2After drive.mount("/content/drive"), where should you save a results file so you can find it tomorrow?

  • That's the runtime's own disk, which is wiped when the runtime ends.

  • Anything under /content/drive/MyDrive is really in your Google Drive.

  • Colab autosaves the notebook, not the files your code writes.

Show answer

B. Anything under /content/drive/MyDrive is really in your Google Drive.

Key takeaways

  • Your code runs on the runtime, a temporary machine. Its working folder is /content.
  • Upload with the Files panel or files.upload(); download with the file's menu or files.download().
  • Mount Drive with drive.mount("/content/drive") and keep data and results under /content/drive/MyDrive.
  • Check every load with shape and head(), and every save by reading the file back.

  • Markdown Guide: Basic Syntax (opens in a new tab): everything you can write in a Colab text cell.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why the same cell can give a different answer the second time you run it.
  • Use Restart session and run all to prove a notebook works from scratch.
  • Lay out a notebook so someone else can follow it from the top.
  • Read a pandas traceback from the bottom and find the real cause.
  • Share notebooks without leaking data you shouldn't.

Here's a notebook cell that takes 10% off three lunch prices. Run it once and the prices look right:

Now suppose you click that second cell again, maybe because you edited a comment. Here's the same code, run a second time:

Pizza now costs 3.24, a 19% discount. Nothing in the code changed. What changed is the runtime's memory: the second run started from the already-discounted prices. If you saved the notebook now and sent it to a friend, their run would show 3.60, and neither of you would know why your numbers disagree.

#The page you see is not the memory the code uses

A notebook has two separate things in it. The page is the cells and outputs you see. The runtime's memory holds every variable that currently exists. They only match if you ran every cell exactly once, from top to bottom.

Three things give the mismatch away:

  • The [n] numbers beside cells. On a clean run they go 1, 2, 3 from the top. A notebook showing [7], [3], [12] was run out of order.
  • Deleted cells. Deleting a cell removes it from the page, but whatever it created stays in memory until the runtime restarts. Your notebook can depend on a cell that no longer exists.
  • Cells that overwrite their own input, like prices = prices * 0.9. Each run changes the answer.

The fix for that last one is to give the result a new name. This cell reloads the original prices and stores the discount separately, so it prints the same thing however many times you run it:

#The clean-restart test

There's one reliable way to know your notebook works: wipe the memory and run everything from the top. In Colab, open Runtime › Restart session and run all. (Older tutorials call it "Restart runtime"; the idea is the same.) Colab clears every variable, then runs each cell in order.

If it finishes without errors and the outputs match what you expected, the notebook is reproducible: anyone who opens it gets the same results. If a cell fails, you've found a hidden dependency, like a variable from a deleted cell or a file that was uploaded by hand. Fix it now, while you still remember what you did.

Do this before you share a notebook, before you submit any project in this course, and whenever results look "weird". In JupyterLab the same command is Kernel › Restart Kernel and Run All Cells.

⚠️ Watch out

A restart doesn't delete files in /content the way a runtime shutdown does, but Runtime › Disconnect and delete runtime does. If your notebook reads an uploaded file, the cleanest test is to disconnect, reconnect, and run all. If it breaks, load the file from Drive instead (the previous lesson shows how).

#Lay out a notebook so it reads top to bottom

A good analysis notebook reads like a short report. Use the same skeleton every time and you'll never hunt for where something happens:

  1. A title text cell: the question you're answering, where the data came from, and the date.
  2. One imports cell: every import in one place, at the top.
  3. One load cell: read the data. Every later cell works from this.
  4. One step per section: a text cell with a ## heading ("Remove duplicate responses"), then the code cells for that step.
  5. A results section: the final tables and charts, with a sentence or two on what they show.

Name files so they sort sensibly in Drive: m2-survey-first-look.ipynb beats Untitled7.ipynb. When you open a notebook from someone else's link, it's read-only for you, so use File › Save a copy in Drive before editing. To keep a copy on your own computer, use File › Download › Download .ipynb.

💡 Tip

The Table of contents icon in the left sidebar builds a clickable outline from your # and ## headings. If the outline looks messy, the notebook is messy.

#Getting unstuck: read the error from the bottom

pandas errors can be 40 lines long, but almost all of that is pandas' own code. The line that matters is the last one. Here's the most common error in this whole course:

Skip to the bottom: KeyError: 'rating'. A KeyError means "there's no column with that exact name." When the name looks right, print the real column names:

There it is: 'rating ' has a trailing space, which often happens when a CSV header was typed by hand. You can rename it, or clean every name at once with survey.columns = survey.columns.str.strip().

When you're stuck, work through this list in order:

  1. Read the last line of the error. Name the error type and the value it complains about.
  2. Check what you actually have. print(df.columns.tolist()), df.dtypes, df.shape, type(x). Most bugs are a gap between what you think a variable holds and what it holds.
  3. Read the docs for the function. In Colab, run pd.read_csv? in a cell to see its documentation, or help(pd.read_csv) anywhere.
  4. Search the last line of the error, in quotes, along with "pandas".
  5. Make it smaller. Copy the failing line into a new cell with a three-row DataFrame. If it works there, the problem is in your data, not your code.

📝 Note

Colab has built-in AI features (Google says they require an account aged 18 or older). If you use any AI helper, ask it to explain the error rather than rewrite your notebook, then make the fix yourself and check the output. You're here to learn to see what's wrong.

#Share notebooks without leaking data

When you share a Colab notebook, the person gets the whole page: code, text, and every output. If a cell printed df.head() on a file of classmates' names and emails, those names and emails are in the shared notebook even after you delete the file. Before sharing:

  • Use Edit › Clear all outputs if outputs might contain personal data, or don't print raw rows of sensitive files at all.
  • Never paste passwords or API keys into cells.
  • Use only data you have permission to use. The datasets in this course are made up or come bundled with the libraries, so they're safe to share.

#How the rest of this course works

Each of Modules 2 to 7 has three lessons. Notes teach the ideas with code you can run. The Build-along uses them to make one real thing, step by step. Practice gives you new problems with hints and full solutions. Module 8 is a capstone: your own data investigation, start to finish. Make one notebook per lesson, and type the code yourself rather than pasting it. It's slower, and it's how the patterns stick.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A cell contains scores = scores + 5. You run it three times by accident. What happened to scores?

  • The code is the same, but each run starts from the value the previous run left in memory.

  • Each run adds 5 to the current value. Writing curved = scores + 5 would avoid the problem.

  • Colab never stops you from rerunning a cell.

Show answer

B. Each run adds 5 to the current value. Writing curved = scores + 5 would avoid the problem.

2Your notebook works when you run cells one by one, but Restart session and run all fails with NameError: name 'clean' is not defined. What's the most likely cause?

  • Memory kept the old variable, so step-by-step runs worked. A fresh start exposes the missing step.

  • It runs every code cell in order; that's what makes it a fair test.

  • A missing library gives ModuleNotFoundError. NameError means a variable or function doesn't exist yet.

Show answer

A. Memory kept the old variable, so step-by-step runs worked. A fresh start exposes the missing step.

3df["Price"] raises KeyError: 'Price', but the CSV clearly has a price column. What should you run first?

  • The library works fine; the error is about a column name.

  • It shows the exact names, including case and stray spaces, such as 'price' or 'Price '.

  • Missing values don't cause a KeyError.

Show answer

B. It shows the exact names, including case and stray spaces, such as 'price' or 'Price '.

Key takeaways

  • The page and the runtime's memory are different things; out-of-order runs and deleted cells make them disagree.
  • Don't let a cell overwrite its own input; give results new names.
  • Restart session and run all is the test for a working notebook. Run it before you share or submit.
  • Read errors from the last line up, then check what your variables really hold.
  • Shared notebooks include outputs, so clear them or avoid printing personal data.

  • The Jupyter Notebook documentation (opens in a new tab): how cells, kernels, and outputs fit together, which applies to Colab as well.
  • Ten simple rules for writing and sharing computational analyses in Jupyter Notebooks (opens in a new tab): a short paper by scientists on keeping notebooks readable and reproducible.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a CSV file stores everything as text and how read_csv decides each column's type.
  • Load nested JSON records with pd.json_normalize and compare them with a CSV export.
  • Run the first-look checklist: shape, head, dtypes, info, describe, value_counts, isna.
  • Find the values that make a numeric-looking column load as text.

The student council ran a sleep and screen-time survey and exported the answers as a CSV file. You load it and ask the simplest possible question, the average hours of sleep:

The last line of the error is the clue: can only concatenate str. pandas tried to add up the sleep hours and found strings. The column looks like numbers on screen, but pandas loaded it as text, so "averaging" it meant gluing words together. This lesson is about catching that before it bites. (io.StringIO wraps a string so read_csv can treat it like a file. With a real file you'd pass its name instead.)

#A CSV file is only text

Open any CSV in a text editor and you'll see what it really is: lines of characters, with commas between values and the first line naming the columns. Nothing in the file says "this column holds numbers". Here is a tiny CSV reader written in plain Python. Step through it and watch the type of every value:

'7.5' is the three characters 7, dot, 5, not the number 7.5. pd.read_csv does the same splitting, then makes an extra pass over each column: if every value in the column can be read as a whole number, the column becomes int64; if they all read as decimals, float64; otherwise the column stays as text, which pandas calls object. A handful of strings, including an empty cell, NA, N/A, NaN, and null, are treated as missing and become NaN ("not a number"), the marker pandas uses for a missing value.

That explains the crash. sleep_hours contains 7 hrs, which isn't a number, so the whole column stayed as text.

#JSON keeps numbers, true/false, and nesting

The same survey app can also export JSON. JSON writes numbers without quotes, has real true/false and null values, and can nest one record inside another or hold a list:

json_normalize turned the nested sleep object into two columns, sleep.hours and sleep.bedtime. Because JSON numbers aren't quoted, screen_hours arrived as float64 with no guessing, phone_in_bedroom is a real bool, and null became NaN. The clubs lists stay as lists inside single cells, which you'd handle later by counting them or splitting them out.

CSV JSON
Shape Flat grid: rows and columns Records, which can nest and hold lists
Types Everything is text; pandas guesses Numbers, strings, true/false, null are explicit
Missing values Empty cell or text like N/A null, or the key is left out
Size Small: names appear once, in the header Bigger: every record repeats every key
Load with pd.read_csv pd.json_normalize(json.loads(...)) or pd.read_json

pd.read_json works well for flat JSON. For nested records like these, it would leave whole dictionaries sitting in a sleep column, so json_normalize is the better tool.

#The first-look checklist

Every time you load a dataset, run the same few checks before you calculate anything. Back to the CSV export:

grade is int64, as it should be. But sleep_hours and screen_hours, which are obviously numbers, are object. Two numeric columns loaded as text is the single most common problem in real data. info() puts types and missing values side by side:

The Non-Null Count column says sleep_hours has 10 real values out of 12 (the empty cell and N/A became NaN), and club is missing for 3 students. Notice that info() prints its report itself, so you call it without print.

Now watch describe(), which summarizes numeric columns:

describe() reported only grade. It didn't complain about sleep or screen time; it silently skipped them, because they're text. If you'd only looked at this table you might never notice two columns were missing. value_counts() is the matching tool for categories: 8 students keep a phone in the bedroom, 4 don't.

#Find the values that turn a column into text

pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") converts what it can and replaces anything unreadable with NaN. Comparing before and after shows exactly which values are the problem:

Two culprits: 7 hrs and 8+. Each one needs a human decision. 7 hrs clearly means 7. 8+ means "at least 8", which isn't the same as 8. You'll fix values like these properly in Module 4. For now, look at what's left once they're set aside:

The right-hand chart is worth making for every new dataset. A quarter of the sleep answers can't be used yet, which matters a lot more than any average you compute from the rest.

⚠️ Watch out

Three loading mistakes to recognize on sight.

  • Everything lands in one column. The file uses semicolons, common in countries where the comma is the decimal mark. df.shape shows 1 column and the header is one long string like student_id;grade;sleep_hours. Fix: pd.read_csv(path, sep=";"), adding decimal="," if numbers look like 7,5.
  • The first data row became the header. Some exports have no header line, so pandas used the first row's values as column names. Fix: header=None, then set df.columns = [...] yourself.
  • df.info without parentheses prints a description of the method instead of the report. Methods need (); attributes like shape and dtypes don't.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A column of prices loads as object. What's the most likely reason?

  • Decimals load fine as float64.

  • One unreadable value keeps the whole column as text.

  • Missing values become NaN, and the column stays numeric (as float64).

Show answer

B. One unreadable value keeps the whole column as text.

2You run survey.describe() on a table with five number-like columns, and it reports only two of them. What should you check next?

  • It shows every numeric column. Fewer than expected is a warning sign.

  • describe() skips text columns without saying so.

  • The file format doesn't change what describe() reports for a DataFrame.

Show answer

B. describe() skips text columns without saying so.

3Which export would load phone_in_bedroom as a real bool with no extra work?

  • To read_csv, yes and no are just text.

  • JSON has a boolean type, and pandas keeps it.

  • pandas has bool, as app.dtypes showed.

Show answer

B. JSON has a boolean type, and pandas keeps it.

Key takeaways

  • A CSV is text. read_csv guesses each column's type, and one unreadable value keeps the whole column as object.
  • JSON stores real numbers, booleans, and null, and can nest; pd.json_normalize flattens nested records into columns.
  • First look, every time: shape, head(), dtypes, info(), describe(), value_counts(), isna().sum().
  • describe() skips text columns silently, so compare its output with dtypes.
  • pd.to_numeric(col, errors="coerce") finds the values that need a decision.

What you'll learn

  • Load a CSV export and a nested JSON export of the same survey and give them matching column names.
  • Write problem_values(), which lists the entries that stop a column from being numeric.
  • Write first_look(), a one-row-per-column report you can reuse on any dataset.
  • Chart how much of each column is usable, and check where the two exports disagree.

Your school surveyed 40 students about their trip to school. The answers exist twice: a CSV from the paper-style web form, where students typed their own numbers, and a JSON export from a commute app that recorded the same trips. Before anyone averages anything, you need to know which file to trust and what's wrong with each. You'll build a report that answers that in one call:

#Step 1: Create the two export files

In real life you'd upload the exports (Module 1 showed how). Here, this cell plays the part of the survey website and writes both files into the runtime. Run it and move on; the interesting work starts in Step 2.

#Step 2: Read the raw CSV, then load it

Look at the file as text first. It takes one line, and it shows you things read_csv will hide:

Already you can see 15 min and a lone -. Now load it and check the types:

Every column is object. Even grade and late_days, which are small whole numbers, loaded as text. Somewhere in each column there's at least one value read_csv couldn't read as a number.

#Step 3: Load the JSON and match the column names

The nested trip object became trip.mode, trip.distance_km, and trip.minutes. To compare the two files column by column, give the JSON columns the CSV's names, then put them in the same order:

The JSON gives you real numbers straight away. minutes is float64 rather than int64 because one reading is NaN, and NaN only exists as a float.

#Step 4: List the values that block a number column

Here's the trick from the Notes lesson turned into a function. It returns the distinct entries that are present but won't convert:

Read the list for minutes carefully, because each item needs a different decision. 15 min and about 20 carry a usable number. 20-25 is a range. And - isn't an answer at all: it's how this form marks "no answer". pandas only treats certain strings as missing, and - isn't one of them, so tell read_csv about it:

- moved from "problem" to "missing", which is where it belongs. That's the only fix you make in this lesson. Repairing 15 min and friends is a cleaning job, and cleaning comes in Module 4, once you know exactly what's broken.

#Step 5: Build the first-look report

Now combine every check into one function. For each column it records the type, how many values are filled and missing, how many are distinct, what share of the filled values read as numbers, and how many rows are unreadable: filled in, but not a number in a column that's mostly numbers.

The two reports tell the story at a glance. In the CSV, student_id and mode have a numeric share of 0, so they're genuinely text and nothing is flagged. The four number columns are 92 to 98% numbers with a few stray entries, which is exactly the pattern of "numbers with typing mistakes". The JSON report has no problems at all, just two missing readings.

The 0.8 threshold is a judgment call. A column where only half the values are numbers is probably a text column with some numbers in it, and listing "problems" there would be noise.

#Step 6: Chart how much of each column you can use

A table of counts is precise; a chart makes the comparison instant. Add missing and unreadable together, since you can't compute with either:

The iloc[::-1] flips the row order so the chart lists columns top to bottom in the same order as the table.

#Step 7: Check whether the two files agree

Fewer problems doesn't prove the JSON is right. Line the two distance_km columns up by student and plot one against the other. If the files agree, every point sits on the diagonal:

set_index("student_id") makes pandas line rows up by student rather than by position, so the subtraction compares each student's two answers even if the files were in different orders. One student typed 68 for a 6.8 km trip. That value was a perfectly valid number, so first_look couldn't catch it. Only comparing with a second source, or a sanity range, can. Hold that thought for Module 4.

#The finished program

Here's everything in one cell, ready to reuse. Change the two file names and it reports on any pair of exports with the same columns:

The rename now uses a function, name.removeprefix("trip."), which strips the prefix from every nested column at once. It's shorter than the dictionary and keeps working if the app adds more trip. fields.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why reload the CSV with na_values=["-"] instead of counting - as a problem value?

  • It loads fine, as plain text; that's why it slipped through.

  • Missing and mistyped values need different fixes. Labeling - correctly keeps the problem list honest.

  • It only changes which strings count as missing; columns with other text stay object.

Show answer

B. Missing and mistyped values need different fixes. Labeling - correctly keeps the problem list honest.

2Why does first_look skip the problem list for columns with a numeric share under 0.8?

  • For mode, every entry fails to convert, and that's correct. Flagging them would bury the real issues.

  • With errors="coerce" it runs on anything and returns NaN where it can't convert.

  • Speed isn't the reason; the report would be noisy and misleading.

Show answer

A. For mode, every entry fails to convert, and that's correct. Flagging them would bury the real issues.

3The student who typed 68 for 6.8 km: why didn't first_look flag that row?

  • The column type doesn't matter here; the value itself is the issue.

  • Plausible-looking wrong numbers need range checks or a second source, like the scatter plot.

  • It checks every column, and it flagged 1.5km in this one.

Show answer

B. Plausible-looking wrong numbers need range checks or a second source, like the scatter plot.

Key takeaways

  • Look at the raw text of a file before loading it; a few lines reveal markers like - and units like km.
  • Tell read_csv about the file's own missing-value markers with na_values.
  • pd.json_normalize plus a rename gives JSON exports the same column names as their CSV twins.
  • first_look() reports type, filled, missing, unique, numeric share, and unreadable values for any DataFrame.
  • Aligning on an ID with set_index compares records by who they belong to, not by row position.
  • A report finds values that aren't numbers; only range checks or a second source find wrong numbers.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a range entry to the report with each numeric column's minimum and maximum, so 68 km would stand out.
  • Add an example entry that shows one filled value per column.
  • Make first_look draw the bar chart itself when called with chart=True.

What you'll learn

  • Predict the dtype read_csv will choose for each column, then check.
  • Fix separator, decimal, and leading-zero problems with read_csv options.
  • Flatten JSON that nests a list of records inside each record.
  • Find the exact values that keep a column from being numeric.
  • Use value_counts and a chart to see what describe hides.

Every exercise uses a small file written inline with io.StringIO, so you can paste each one into Colab as-is. Work in one notebook and run this setup cell first.

#Warm-up: predict the dtypes

Before running anything, write down the dtype you expect for each of the four columns. One of them will probably surprise you.

aisle holds whole numbers, but it's float64. Eggs has no aisle, the blank becomes NaN, and NaN is a float, so the whole column becomes float. Meanwhile True/False text does load as real booleans, while yes/no wouldn't.

#Exercise 1: Size up a library log

Load the checkout log below. Print its shape, its dtypes, and how many books have no due date.

Need a hint?

isna() gives True/False for each value, and sum() counts the Trues.

Show solution

Notice that both date columns are object. read_csv doesn't turn text into dates unless you ask (with parse_dates=["checked_out", "due_date"]), so for now they're strings that happen to look like dates.

#Exercise 2: A file that loads as one column

A weather station in Lyon, France, exports this file. Load it so that temp_c and rain_mm are numbers, then print the mean temperature and total rain.

Need a hint?

Load it plainly first and print .shape. Then look up two read_csv options: one for what goes between values, and one for the character inside numbers.

Show solution

The plain load has 1 column because there's no comma between fields. sep=";" splits the fields, and decimal="," reads 8,4 as 8.4. Without decimal, the temperatures would stay text.

#Exercise 3: The vanishing zeros

A club roster has ZIP codes and phone numbers. Load it and print it. What happened to Ana's ZIP code? Fix the load so it matches the file exactly.

Need a hint?

Is a ZIP code a quantity you'd ever average? read_csv takes a dtype= dictionary that maps column names to types.

Show solution

02139 looked like a number, so pandas read it as the integer 2139 and the leading zero was gone. ZIP codes, phone numbers, and ID numbers are labels made of digits. You'll never add them up, so load them as str. Any column where a leading zero matters needs this.

#Exercise 4: Orders with a list of items inside

An online bookstore exports orders as JSON. Each order holds a list of items. Build a table with one row per item that also shows the order ID and customer city. Then add a line_total column (qty × price) and print the total sales.

Need a hint?

Plain pd.json_normalize(records) gives one row per order, with the items list stuck in a single cell. Look at the record_path and meta parameters. A nested field in meta is written as a list of keys: ["customer", "city"].

Show solution

record_path="items" tells pandas which list to unroll, so 3 orders become 5 rows. meta copies fields from the parent order onto each of its rows, so every item knows which order and city it came from.

#Exercise 5: Find the values that aren't prices

A bake-sale sheet has a price column that loads as object. Print each entry that's filled in but can't be read as a number, with its row number.

Need a hint?

Convert with pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce"). A value is a culprit if it's missing after converting but wasn't missing before.

Show solution

The pie row is None, so it's missing both before and after, and the second condition leaves it out. Each culprit needs a different fix: strip the $, decide whether free means 0, and swap the decimal comma.

#Exercise 6: The average rating that nobody gave

Twenty people rated a new cafeteria menu from 1 to 5. Print describe(), then make a bar chart of how many people gave each rating, including any rating nobody chose. What does the chart show that the mean hides?

Need a hint?

value_counts() skips values that never appear. .reindex(range(1, 6), fill_value=0) puts them back with a count of 0.

Show solution

The mean is 3.4, which sounds like "people thought it was okay". The chart says the opposite: almost everyone either loved it (11 fives) or hated it (7 ones). Nobody chose 3. A single summary number can describe a group that doesn't exist, so always look at the distribution of a column, not just its average.

#Challenge: Do the CSV and JSON exports match?

A fundraiser exports its donations twice. Write code that prints (a) donor IDs that appear in only one file, and (b) every column whose dtype differs between the two files, side by side.

Need a hint?

Python sets support - for "in this set but not that one". For dtypes, pd.DataFrame({"csv": a.dtypes, "json": b.dtypes}) builds a side-by-side table; keep the rows where the two columns differ.

Show solution

D4 is missing from the JSON and D5 from the CSV, so neither file alone has every donation. The dtype table explains two traps: amount is int64 in one file and float64 in the other (harmless for math, but worth knowing), and recurring is the text yes/no in the CSV but a real bool in the JSON. Code that does df[df["recurring"]] works on the JSON version and fails on the CSV.

What you'll learn

  • Explain why vectorized NumPy math beats a Python loop, and measure the difference.
  • Create arrays, do math on them, and summarize along an axis.
  • Filter with boolean masks, combining conditions with & and |.
  • Select data with [], loc, and iloc, and add new columns.
  • Summarize groups with groupby().agg() and join two tables with merge.

A weather network logs a million temperature readings in Fahrenheit, and your team needs them in Celsius. The first draft is the loop you'd write in any Python class. The second is one line of NumPy. Both produce the same million numbers:

The exact times depend on the computer, but the gap is always large, often well over 20 times. A million values is a small dataset by data-science standards, and the gap grows with the data. This lesson is about writing that second version by habit.

#Why the loop is slow

Step through the loop version on four readings. Each pass, Python fetches one value, works out what type it is, does three operations, and appends the result to a list:

All of that bookkeeping happens again for every single value. A NumPy array is different: it's one block of memory holding numbers of one type, so NumPy can run the arithmetic for every element inside fast, compiled C code, with no per-item Python work. Doing math on a whole array at once is called vectorization.

#Arrays: one type, one shape, math on everything

Two things to notice. Arithmetic on an array applies to every element, while the same operator on a list does list things (* repeats it). And axis picks the direction to summarize: axis=1 collapses across columns, giving one answer per row, while axis=0 collapses down the rows, giving one answer per column.

#Boolean masks pick values by a condition

Comparing an array with a value gives an array of True/False the same size, called a mask. Masks do three jobs:

hot.sum() counts, hot.mean() gives a proportion, and celsius[hot] filters. Combine conditions with & (and), | (or), and ~ (not), and wrap each comparison in parentheses, because & binds more tightly than >.

⚠️ Watch out

Python's and and or don't work on arrays or columns:

and needs a single True or False, and an array of a million answers isn't one. The message suggests a.any() or a.all(), but what you almost always want is &. The same error appears with pandas columns, worded as "The truth value of a Series is ambiguous".

#pandas keeps the labels attached

NumPy arrays are fast but anonymous: position 0 is just position 0. That gets dangerous as soon as two lists come in different orders. Here are two days of readings from three stations, where Tuesday's file happens to be sorted differently:

The NumPy subtraction paired Hilltop's Tuesday with Airport's Monday and reported a 7.4-degree drop that never happened. The pandas version aligns on the index: each value is matched by its label, whatever order the data arrives in. A Series is a NumPy array plus labels, and a DataFrame is a table of Series that share one index.

Here's a month of daily readings from four stations, 120 rows:

A new column is just a vectorized expression on existing columns, assigned to a new name. np.where makes a column from a condition:

To select, use loc with labels and conditions and iloc with positions:

loc[rows, columns] reads like a sentence: "the rows where it's over 34 °C, and these three columns". iloc slices by position like a list, so 0:2 means positions 0 and 1. Prefer loc in analysis code, because column positions change when someone adds a column.

#Group, summarize, and join

"What's the average temperature at each station?" is a three-step idea called split-apply-combine:

Station names alone don't tell you why Downtown runs hot. A second table, kept by the city, describes each station. merge joins the two on their shared column:

on="station" names the key, and how="left" keeps every row of the left table even if a station is missing from the info table (its new columns would be NaN). reset_index() turned station back from the index into an ordinary column so merge could find it. Now the pattern has an explanation you can check: Hilltop, at 140 m, is the coolest.

⚠️ Watch out

Changing a filtered copy changes nothing. weather[weather["station"] == "Hilltop"]["temp_c"] = 0 looks like it sets Hilltop's temperatures, but the first [...] makes a temporary copy, and the assignment goes into the copy. pandas may print a SettingWithCopyWarning, and weather is unchanged. Always do conditional assignment in one loc call: weather.loc[weather["station"] == "Hilltop", "temp_c"] = 0.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1a = np.array([2, 4, 6]). What does a[a > 3].sum() give?

  • a > 3 is [False, True, True], and sum() of the mask alone would be 2. Here the mask filters a first.

  • The mask keeps 4 and 6, and their sum is 10.

  • That's the sum of the whole array; the mask removed the 2.

Show answer

B. The mask keeps 4 and 6, and their sum is 10.

2Which line correctly selects rainy days at the Harbor station?

  • and fails on columns with "truth value ... is ambiguous".

  • Without parentheses, & runs before == and pandas raises an error.

  • Each comparison makes a mask, and & combines them element by element.

Show answer

C. Each comparison makes a mask, and & combines them element by element.

3Two Series hold the same stations in different orders. Why does b - a still pair each station correctly?

  • The labels, not the positions, decide which values meet.

  • Sorting isn't what happens; it matches labels, and the result's order is a side effect.

  • to_numpy() throws the labels away, which is exactly what causes mismatches.

Show answer

A. The labels, not the positions, decide which values meet.

4weather.groupby("station")["rain_mm"].agg(["sum", "count"]) returns how many rows?

  • groupby combines each group into one row.

  • There are four stations, so four groups, each summarized into one row.

  • The statistics become columns, not rows.

Show answer

B. There are four stations, so four groups, each summarized into one row.

Key takeaways

  • Vectorized NumPy math runs in compiled code and is usually tens of times faster than a Python loop.
  • Arithmetic and comparisons apply to every element; axis chooses rows or columns for summaries.
  • A boolean mask counts (sum), measures a share (mean), and filters (arr[mask]). Combine masks with &, |, ~ and parentheses.
  • pandas aligns by label, which keeps each value attached to the row it belongs to.
  • loc selects by label or condition, iloc by position. Assign conditionally with a single loc.
  • groupby().agg() is split-apply-combine; merge(on=..., how="left") joins tables on a shared key.

#Further reading

  • NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners (opens in a new tab): arrays, shapes, axes, and masks, from the NumPy team.
  • pandas: How do I select a subset of a DataFrame? (opens in a new tab): [], loc, and iloc with clear pictures.
  • pandas: Group by: split-apply-combine (opens in a new tab): the full guide, including agg, transform, and filter.

What you'll learn

  • Compute a new column from two datetime columns without a loop.
  • Remove impossible rows with a boolean mask and keep a record of how many went.
  • Summarize every station at once with groupby and named aggregations.
  • Join a lookup table with merge and use it to compare stations fairly.
  • Chart trips per dock and riders by hour.

A city bike-share runs ten stations. The operations team has one month of trip records, 5,000 rows, and one question: which stations need more docks? Last year someone answered it by hand in a spreadsheet, copying totals station by station, and the numbers never matched the next time anyone checked. You'll build the answer as code, so it reruns in a second on next month's file.

#Step 1: Load a month of trips

The cell below generates the month of trips with a fixed random seed, so your numbers will match this page exactly. With real data, this is where pd.read_csv would go.

Each row is one ride: when it started and ended, where, who rode (a member with a yearly pass or a casual rider), and how far.

#Step 2: Compute every trip's length at once

Subtracting two datetime columns gives a column of time spans. .dt.total_seconds() turns each span into seconds, for all 5,000 rows in one expression:

Always read min and max first. A trip of -5 minutes ended before it started, and 1800 minutes is 30 hours on a bike. These are clock glitches, not rides. A mask keeps only believable trips, and printing the count keeps the decision visible:

~believable flips the mask, so its sum counts the rows being dropped. The .copy() makes trips a real, independent table instead of a view into the old one, which lets you add columns in the next step without pandas warnings.

#Step 3: Add the columns the questions need

Each new column is one vectorized expression:

casual and round_trip are boolean columns. Storing a yes/no fact as True/False pays off in the next step, because the mean of a boolean column is the share of True values and its sum is the count.

The quick groupby at the end already says something useful: members ride faster and shorter. They're commuting; casual riders are touring.

#Step 4: Summarize every station in one call

Named aggregation lets you choose a name, a column, and a function for each result column. That turns 5,000 rows into a 10-row table:

Read each line inside agg as "new column = (source column, function)". casual_share is the mean of a True/False column, so it's a proportion: about 30% of rides at most stations are casual. Union Sq is by far the busiest station.

But is Union Sq the most crowded? Not necessarily. A station with 40 docks can handle far more trips than one with 15. To answer the real question you need each station's size, and that lives in a different table.

#Step 5: Merge in station details

The city's station table has one row per station:

Three choices in that chain are worth naming. reset_index() turns the station names from the index back into a column. rename gives that column the same name as in stations, so on="station" can match them. And validate="one_to_one" makes merge raise an error if either table has a station listed twice, which would otherwise quietly duplicate rows and inflate every total.

The ranking flips. Union Sq handles the most trips, but it also has the most docks. College Ave, with only 15 docks, works each dock hardest. Stadium, with 30 docks and few riders, has spare capacity that could move.

#Step 6: When do people ride?

Group by two keys and count the rows in each pair with size(). unstack() then turns the inner key, rider type, into columns, which is exactly the shape a line chart wants:

Members produce the two rush-hour peaks, and casual riders own the early afternoon. For the operations team, this means docks at commuter stations fill and empty fastest from 7 to 9 a.m. and around 5 p.m.

#The finished program

Everything after the data generation, in one function. It starts from the untouched raw_trips saved in Step 1. Point it at next month's trips and station tables and it produces the same report:

The function works on a copy of the trips table, so calling it never changes the data you pass in. Running it twice gives the same answer, which is the reproducibility habit from Module 1 built into the code.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the report rank stations by trips_per_dock rather than by trips?

  • The counts are fine; they just answer a different question.

  • Dividing by capacity compares stations of different sizes fairly. That's why College Ave rises to the top.

  • merge keeps every column from both tables.

Show answer

B. Dividing by capacity compares stations of different sizes fairly. That's why College Ave rises to the top.

2What would validate="one_to_one" catch?

  • The merge would duplicate that station's row and double-count it. validate raises an error instead.

  • A station missing from the trips just wouldn't appear in the left table; that's not a one-to-one violation.

  • That raises a KeyError with or without validate.

Show answer

A. The merge would duplicate that station's row and double-count it. validate raises an error instead.

3casual_share=("casual", "mean") gives 0.31 for Union Sq. What does that mean?

  • casual is True/False, not a time.

  • True counts as 1 and False as 0, so the mean is the share of True.

  • Docks aren't involved until after the merge.

Show answer

B. True counts as 1 and False as 0, so the mean is the share of True.

Key takeaways

  • Datetime columns subtract like numbers; .dt.total_seconds() and .dt.hour pull out parts for every row at once.
  • Drop impossible rows with a mask, and print how many you dropped.
  • Store yes/no facts as booleans, so mean gives a share and sum gives a count.
  • Named aggregation (new=("column", "function")) builds a clean summary table in one call.
  • merge(..., validate="one_to_one") joins lookup data safely; normalizing by it (trips per dock) can reverse a ranking.
  • groupby([a, b]).size().unstack() reshapes counts into a chart-ready table.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Count trips by end station too, and find stations where more bikes arrive than leave. Those are the stations where bikes pile up.
  • Split trips_per_dock into weekday and weekend using start_time.dt.dayofweek >= 5.
  • Add a neighborhood summary: group report by neighborhood and sum trips and docks before dividing.

  • pandas: Merge, join, concatenate and compare (opens in a new tab): every join type, with diagrams of which rows survive.
  • pandas: Time deltas (opens in a new tab): what you get when you subtract datetimes, and how to convert it.

Run the setup cell once, then work through the exercises in order. Try each one before opening the hint, and open the solution only after you have output of your own to compare.

#Warm-up: arrays vs. lists

Predict all three lines before you run them:

Arrays multiply element by element ([1 4 9]), lists repeat, and adding a single number to an array adds it to every element. That last behavior is called broadcasting.

#Exercise 1: Delete the loop

A shop computes each line's total, with 8% tax, using a loop. Rewrite the calculation as one NumPy expression and check that every answer matches.

Need a hint?

Turn both lists into arrays with np.array(...). Then the same formula works on all five lines at once. np.allclose(a, b) checks that two sets of decimals agree.

Show solution

p * q multiplies matching positions, * 1.08 broadcasts the tax onto every line, and .round(2) rounds all five at once. No list, no append, no index.

#Exercise 2: Questions about 200 exam scores

Using the scores below, print: (a) how many scores are 90 or above, (b) the share of scores from 70 to 80 inclusive, and (c) the average of the failing scores (below 60) and how many there are.

Need a hint?

Each question is a mask. .sum() counts it, .mean() turns it into a share, and scores[mask] keeps only the matching scores. For "between", combine two comparisons with & and wrap each in parentheses.

Show solution

The mask failing is used twice: summed to count the failing scores, and as a filter to average them. Naming a mask makes code like this easier to read.

#Exercise 3: loc, iloc, and a sort

Load the planets table below, with the planet name as the index. Then:

  1. Get the number of moons of Mars, by label.
  2. Get the first three rows and first two columns, by position.
  3. Sort by moons, most first. What does iloc[0] give now, and does loc["Earth"] still work?
Need a hint?

loc[row_label, column_label] and iloc[row_positions, column_positions]. After sorting, positions change but labels stay with their rows.

Show solution

After the sort, position 0 is Saturn, not Mercury, but loc["Earth"] still finds Earth because the label travels with its row. This is why loc is safer in analysis code: code that says which row you mean keeps working when the order changes. (The moon counts are NASA's 2023 figures. Astronomers keep finding small moons, so newer counts are higher, especially for Saturn.)

#Exercise 4: Columns from rules

Add three columns to planets:

  • vs_earth: each diameter divided by Earth's diameter, rounded to 2 places.
  • has_moons: "yes" or "no".
  • kind: "rocky" below 15,000 km, "ice giant" from 15,000 to 60,000 km, "gas giant" above that.
Need a hint?

Earth's diameter is planets.loc["Earth", "diameter_km"]. For two outcomes use np.where. For several ranges, pd.cut(column, bins=[...], labels=[...]) sorts each value into a bin.

Show solution

pd.cut uses each bin as "above the left edge, up to and including the right edge", so with 3 bins you need 4 edges. Jupiter is 11.21 Earths across.

#Exercise 5: Which grade won the food drive?

Each homeroom reports how many cans it collected. Grade 11 collected the most cans in total. Is it really the winner? Group by grade and report total cans, number of homerooms, total students, and cans per student, sorted best first. Draw a bar chart of cans per student.

Need a hint?

Use named aggregation: cans=("cans", "sum"), homerooms=("homeroom", "count"), and so on. Compute cans per student after grouping, from the totals.

Show solution

Grade 11 has the biggest total only because it has three homerooms and 85 students. Per student, grade 12 gave the most. Dividing the summed cans by the summed students is the right calculation; averaging each homeroom's per-student rate would weight a 24-student room the same as a 30-student room.

#Exercise 6: Who's missing from the club list?

Join students and signups so that every row from both tables survives. Then list (a) students who signed up for nothing, and (b) signups whose student_id doesn't match any student.

Need a hint?

how="outer" keeps unmatched rows from both sides. indicator=True adds a _merge column whose values are both, left_only, or right_only.

Show solution

Dev and Femi haven't joined anything. Student 107 signed up for Chess but doesn't exist in the student list, probably a typo for a real ID. Notice that Carla appears twice: one student with two clubs gives two rows. A default merge (how="inner") would have silently dropped Dev, Femi, and the 107 signup, and you'd never have known.

#Challenge: Best score, or best compared to their class?

Three teachers gave the same test. Add a class_avg column (each student's own class average, repeated on every row) and a vs_class column (score minus class average). Who has the top score overall, and who is furthest above their own class average? Plot every score by class, with a line at each class average.

Need a hint?

groupby(...).agg(...) shrinks each group to one row. groupby("teacher")["score"].transform("mean") returns one value per original row instead, so you can assign it straight to a new column.

Show solution

The top score overall is in Mr. Chen's class, where everyone scored high. The student furthest above their own class is in Ms. Ortiz's class, with a score that would be ordinary in Mr. Chen's room. Which one is "best" depends on the question, and transform is what lets you ask the second one: it broadcasts a group summary back onto every row.

What you'll learn

  • Convert text columns to real numbers and dates, and read the error when astype refuses.
  • Turn disguised missing values like -999 into NaN, and know what pandas does with NaN by default.
  • Find exact and key-based duplicates.
  • Standardize inconsistent category names.
  • Separate impossible values (errors) from outliers (real but unusual), and reshape a table into tidy form.

A neighborhood group put low-cost air sensors in two areas, Eastside and Northgate, to measure PM2.5, the fine particles in smoke and exhaust, in micrograms per cubic meter. Their first report averaged the readings by neighborhood:

Two neighborhoods became seven. One "average" is negative, which is impossible for a count of particles. One is 1,450, which would mean the air was unbreathable, and two are NaN. The code ran without a single error. Every one of these numbers comes from a data problem the code quietly accepted. This lesson fixes them one at a time, and each fix is a decision you should be able to explain.

#Fix the types first

The pm25 column loaded as text, because one reading says 9.4 ug. You can't compare text with numbers, so types come first. The obvious fix fails loudly:

astype is strict: one bad value and the whole conversion stops. That's useful, because the error names the culprit. Strip the unit, then convert with to_numeric, and convert the time column too:

The result goes into a new column, pm25_num, and the original stays untouched. That keeps the cell safe to run twice, and lets you compare raw and clean values side by side later.

#Missing values come in disguises

pandas knows a value is missing only if it's NaN (or None). Real data hides missing values in other forms: an empty string, N/A, 0, or a sentinel like -999, a number deliberately chosen to be impossible so it means "no reading". Sensor A1's -999 is a sentinel. Left alone, it gets averaged as if it were real air:

Notice count() is smaller than len(). Statistics like mean, sum, and median skip NaN by default, so the mean here is the average of the 11 readings that exist (still inflated by the 1,450 reading, which you'll deal with below). That default is usually what you want, but it's silent. When a quarter of a group's readings are missing, its average rests on far fewer values than the row count suggests.

You have three choices for each gap, and each one changes the answer:

Choice Code When it's reasonable
Leave it as NaN (do nothing) Most of the time; statistics skip it, so report how many are missing
Drop the row df.dropna(subset=["pm25_num"]) The row is useless without that value
Fill it df["pm25_num"].fillna(value) You have a defensible value, like the same sensor's previous reading

Filling with 0 is almost never right for a measurement. Zero particles is a real (and remarkable) reading, not a stand-in for "unknown", and it drags every average down.

#Duplicates: exact and by key

Sensor A2 uploaded its 09:00 reading twice. duplicated() marks every row that repeats an earlier one exactly:

Checking a key (here, sensor plus time) is stricter and usually more useful than exact matching. A sensor can only produce one reading per hour, so two rows with the same key are a duplicate even if one has a typo in another column. keep="first" keeps the earliest copy; keep="last" keeps the latest, which is the right choice when later uploads are corrections.

#Make category names agree

To a computer, Eastside, EASTSIDE, East Side, and eastside are four different strings. Step through the normalizing recipe on three of them:

pandas applies the same three steps to a whole column with the .str methods, and a small dictionary maps each key to the display name you want:

map turns any key that isn't in the dictionary into NaN, so printing the unmapped names is a free safety check. If next month's file says Eastsde, it shows up here instead of silently forming its own group.

#Impossible values and outliers are different things

An impossible value breaks a rule of the world or the instrument. PM2.5 can't be negative, and this sensor model can't report above 1,000. Those values are errors, so they become NaN:

Two clean neighborhoods, believable averages, and a count column that admits how many readings each average rests on. Compare that with the seven-row table at the top.

An outlier is different: a value far from the rest that might be perfectly real. A common rule flags values more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the middle half of the data (the IQR, or interquartile range, is the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles). Here's a month of daily averages from both areas, including two days of wildfire smoke:

The rule flags August 20 and 21 in both places. Deleting them would erase the most important days of the month: the smoke was real, and those are the days people needed to stay inside. Flag outliers and investigate; delete only values that are impossible. When an outlier is real but distorts a summary, report the median alongside the mean, or report results with and without it.

#Tidy data: one row per observation

Cleaning includes shape. Data is tidy when each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value sits in one cell. Spreadsheets often spread one variable across many columns:

In wide, "month" is hidden in the column names, so a question like "average PM2.5 per month" needs a different line of code for every column. melt turns those columns into rows. Now month is an ordinary column, and groupby("month"), filtering, and plotting all just work.

⚠️ Watch out

Three cleaning bugs that don't raise errors.

  • air.drop_duplicates() on its own line returns a new DataFrame and changes nothing. Assign it: air = air.drop_duplicates().
  • df.dropna() with no subset drops a row if any column is missing, including columns you don't care about. Name the column: dropna(subset=["pm25_num"]).
  • fillna(0) on a measurement invents a reading of zero. Leave it missing unless you can defend the fill value.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A column has the values [10, 20, NaN, 30]. What does .mean() return?

  • That divides 60 by 4, treating the missing value as 0.

  • NaN is skipped by default, so it's 60 divided by the 3 real values.

  • That happens only with mean(skipna=False).

Show answer

B. NaN is skipped by default, so it's 60 divided by the 3 real values.

2A temperature column contains -99 on days the sensor was offline. What should you do first?

  • Sentinels must become real missing values before any statistics are computed.

  • The other readings are fine; only the sentinel values are the problem.

  • Check the documentation: an exact repeated value like -99 is a code, not weather.

Show answer

A. Sentinels must become real missing values before any statistics are computed.

3A box plot flags three very high pollution days. Which action is right?

  • If they're real, deleting them hides the most important days in the data.

  • Outliers are worth investigating, not automatically removing.

  • That invents data and hides a real event.

Show answer

B. Outliers are worth investigating, not automatically removing.

4Which table is tidy?

  • The variable "test number" is hidden in the column names.

  • Each variable is a column and each observation (one score) is a row.

  • Students, a variable, are spread across columns.

Show answer

B. Each variable is a column and each observation (one score) is a row.

Key takeaways

  • Fix types first: astype fails loudly on bad values; to_numeric(errors="coerce") and to_datetime convert what they can.
  • Turn disguised missing values (-999, N/A, "") into NaN. Statistics skip NaN silently, so report count() alongside every average.
  • Check duplicates by a key (subset=[...]) as well as exactly.
  • Standardize categories with .str.strip().str.lower() plus a mapping, and print anything left unmapped.
  • Impossible values are errors; outliers may be real. Flag outliers, investigate them, and keep the real ones.
  • Tidy data has one variable per column and one observation per row; melt converts wide tables.

#Further reading

  • pandas: Working with missing data (opens in a new tab): how NaN, None, and pd.NA behave, and every tool for finding and filling gaps.
  • Tidy Data, by Hadley Wickham (opens in a new tab): the paper that defined tidy data, with messy examples you'll recognize.
  • pandas: Reshaping and pivot tables (opens in a new tab): melt, pivot, stack, and unstack with pictures.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Inspect a messy file and record the "before" answer to your question.
  • Clean column names, missing-value markers, units, duplicates, categories, and impossible values in that order.
  • Keep a cleaning log that says what each step changed.
  • Compare the answer before and after cleaning with a chart.
  • Package every step into one reusable function.

Volunteers in three neighborhoods walked their streets in June and recorded every street tree: species, trunk diameter, height, and condition. The city will spend its tree-care budget where trees are in the worst shape, so the question is simple: which neighborhood has the highest share of trees in poor condition? The file the volunteers produced is anything but simple. By the end of this build you'll have a clean table, a log of every change, and an answer you can defend:

The order matters. Types come before range checks, because you can't test height > 60 on text. Duplicates come before categories, so you don't spend effort fixing rows you're about to delete.

#Step 1: Create the survey file

This cell stands in for the volunteers' spreadsheet export. It builds 60 trees, then adds the kinds of mess real surveys have. Run it and treat tree_survey.csv as a file you were handed.

#Step 2: Look before you touch anything

Load the file and get the answer as the data stands. You'll compare against it at the end:

There are 67 rows for 60 trees, Trunk Diameter is text, and Condition has nine spellings of three words, plus unknown. The naive answer is a mess too: five "neighborhoods", one of which (Northgate with a trailing space) has 100% of its trees in poor condition, because it has exactly one tree. Eastside and Riverbend look tied. Hold on to those numbers.

#Step 3: Start the log and fix the column names

Every step will add a line to a log, so anyone reading the notebook can see what changed:

Lowercase names with underscores mean trees["tree_id"] instead of trees["Tree ID"], with no spaces or capitals to mistype. trees is a copy, so raw stays untouched for the final comparison.

#Step 4: Mark the missing values

The volunteers used three different markers for "don't know": ? for diameter, unknown for condition, and -1 for height:

height_m loaded as a number (every entry was numeric text), so -1 is the number −1, not the string "-1". That's why it gets its own replace. Six values are now honestly missing.

#Step 5: Fix types and units

Diameters come as 43, 43cm, or 17 in. Strip the units, convert to numbers, and convert inches to centimeters:

na=False tells endswith to answer False for missing diameters instead of NaN, so the mask stays purely True/False. Without the inch conversion, four trees would be recorded as less than half their real size.

#Step 6: Remove duplicates

There are two kinds. Two rows were uploaded twice, word for word. Five trees were surveyed a second time on June 28, and the later visit is the one to trust:

Sorting by date first is what makes keep="last" mean "keep the latest visit". Without the sort, "last" would just mean "whichever row happened to be lower in the file". is_unique confirms the result: exactly one row per tree.

#Step 7: Make the categories agree

Neighborhoods and conditions only need spacing and capitals fixed. Species names need a lookup table, since Acer rubrum and Maple, red are both Red Maples:

Unmapped species: 0 is the check that the dictionary covered every spelling. If a new survey brings Gingko biloba, that count goes up and tells you to add it. (The changed count also includes the one missing condition, because NaN never equals NaN.)

#Step 8: Remove impossible values

No street tree is 250 meters tall; the tallest trees on Earth are about 115 m, and street trees rarely pass 30. A ceiling of 60 m catches typos without touching any real tree:

Maybe the 250 was meant to be 25.0, or 2.50. But this Ginkgo's trunk is only 20 cm across, which makes even 25 m doubtful, so there's no safe guess. Marking it missing is honest. A guessed value would look exactly like a measured one in the clean table, and nobody reading it would know a guess was made.

#Step 9: Answer the question, before and after

The .dropna() on compare drops the two misspelled neighborhoods, which only exist in the "before" column. Before cleaning, Eastside and Riverbend looked equally bad. After cleaning, Riverbend has the worst trees by a clear margin. Three fixes moved it: two Riverbend trees were recorded as POOR and poor, which the exact match == "Poor" never counted; a June 28 re-survey found another Riverbend tree had declined; and the tree with an unknown condition no longer counts as healthy. The log underneath shows every change that led there.

#The finished program

All the steps as one function. It takes the raw table and returns the clean one plus its log, so the whole cleaning reruns in one call when next year's survey arrives:

The function converts height_m with to_numeric even though this year's file loaded it as numbers. Next year's file might contain a ? in that column, and the function shouldn't break when it does.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the pipeline sort by survey_date before drop_duplicates(subset="tree_id", keep="last")?

  • drop_duplicates works on unsorted data; the sort changes which copy is kept.

  • Without the sort, "last" just means lower in the file, which could be the older visit.

  • Readability is a side effect; the sort decides which condition each tree ends up with.

Show answer

B. Without the sort, "last" just means lower in the file, which could be the older visit.

2The 250 m height might be a slipped decimal point. Why set it to NaN instead of dividing by 10?

  • trees.loc[mask, "height_m"] / 10 works fine.

  • With a 20 cm trunk, even 25 m is doubtful. Marking it missing is honest; if you ever do repair a value, the log must say so.

  • Even unused columns should be correct; someone else may use them.

Show answer

B. With a 20 cm trunk, even 25 m is doubtful. Marking it missing is honest; if you ever do repair a value, the log must say so.

3In Step 9, why are poor-condition shares computed on known (rows with a condition) rather than all trees?

  • NaN == "Poor" is False, which would quietly treat unknown trees as healthy and lower the share.

  • groupby handles them; the issue is what the comparison counts.

  • The goal is accuracy; here it happens to raise the share slightly.

Show answer

A. NaN == "Poor" is False, which would quietly treat unknown trees as healthy and lower the share.

Key takeaways

  • Record the "before" answer first; the comparison shows what cleaning actually changed.
  • Clean in an order that makes each step possible: names, missing markers, types, duplicates, categories, then ranges.
  • Units hide inside text (cm, in); split them out and convert to one unit.
  • Sort before drop_duplicates(keep="last") so "last" means "latest".
  • Map spelling variants with a dictionary and always print the count of unmapped values.
  • A cleaning log and a single clean_...() function make the work repeatable and checkable.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a check that flags trees whose height is unusually large or small for their diameter, rather than only impossible heights.
  • Make clean_tree_survey raise an error if any species is unmapped, so a new spelling can never slip through.
  • Break the after-cleaning poor share down by species within Riverbend. Is one species driving it?

#Further reading

  • pandas: Working with text data (opens in a new tab): every .str method used here, plus extract and split for harder cases.
  • pandas.DataFrame.drop_duplicates reference (opens in a new tab): subset, keep, and ignore_index.
