m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find missing values that hide as -, n/a, or ?, and report how many values each statistic used.
  • Normalize keys before removing duplicates.
  • Turn currency text into numbers.
  • Map category spellings to a fixed set and list what didn't map.
  • Decide what to do with outliers using a rule you can state.
  • Reshape a wide table with melt, and combine every skill in one cleaning function.

Each exercise builds its own tiny dataset inline, so you can paste it into Colab as-is. Run the setup cell first.

#Warm-up: how many values are missing?

Predict both numbers before you run this. Which of the four odd-looking entries does pandas treat as missing on its own?

The empty cells and N/A are on pandas' built-in list of missing markers, so the first count is 3. A lone - isn't on that list, so it only counts once you name it in na_values.

#Exercise 1: Attendance with gaps

A club logs how many sessions each member attended per week. Blank, -, and n/a all mean "not recorded", but 0 means the member was recorded as attending nothing. Load the sheet so that only the unrecorded entries are missing, then print each week's mean and how many members that mean is based on.

Need a hint?

Pass na_values=["-", "n/a"] to read_csv. On the three week columns, .mean() and .count() each give one number per week; put them side by side in a new DataFrame.

Show solution

Each mean uses only 3 of the 4 members, because mean skips NaN. Dee's 0 stays in, which is correct: it's a real record of zero sessions. If you'd filled the gaps with 0, every week's mean would drop and Ana, Ben, and Cy would be marked absent when nobody knows.

#Exercise 2: People who signed up twice

Students order club T-shirts through a form, and some submitted twice. Keep only each person's latest submission. Watch out: the same email can appear with different capitals or a trailing space.

Need a hint?

Count duplicates on the raw email column first; you'll get 0. Clean the key with .str.strip().str.lower(), convert submitted with pd.to_datetime, sort by time, then drop_duplicates(subset="email", keep="last").

Show solution

On the raw column, drop_duplicates finds nothing, because Ben@School.org and ben@school.org are different strings. Normalize the key, then deduplicate. Ana changed her size from M to S and Ben from L to XL, and the latest orders are the ones to send to the printer.

#Exercise 3: Prices stored as text

Convert the price column into a numeric price_usd column. TBD should become missing. Then print the mean price and how many bikes it's based on.

Need a hint?

Remove $ and , with .str.replace(..., "", regex=False), then pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce"). regex=False matters for $, which has a special meaning in patterns.

Show solution

The thousands comma has to go too: pd.to_numeric("1,200") fails, because Python never uses commas inside numbers. The :,.2f format puts commas back for display only.

#Exercise 4: Fifteen ways to write four sizes

Map these shirt sizes to exactly S, M, L, XL. Print any values your mapping misses, then chart the counts in size order, not alphabetical order.

Need a hint?

Normalize with .str.strip().str.lower() first, so your dictionary only needs lowercase keys. After value_counts(), .reindex(["S", "M", "L", "XL"]) puts the bars in the order you choose.

Show solution

XXL isn't a typo for another size; it's a size the form didn't offer. The unmapped list catches it, and someone needs to decide whether to order it. Never let a mapping silently drop a value.

#Exercise 5: Suspicious reaction times

A reaction-time game recorded 45 tries in milliseconds. Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to flag outliers. Then apply two stated rules: under 100 ms is impossible for a human reacting to a signal (the player pressed early), and over 2,000 ms is not a reaction (they looked away). Print the mean and median before and after.

Need a hint?

times.quantile([0.25, 0.75]) gives Q1 and Q3. For the stated rules, one mask does it: (times >= 100) & (times <= 2000).

Show solution

The IQR rule flags five tries, including 610 ms, which is slow but completely possible. That's why a statistical rule should only flag values. The stated rules remove four tries for reasons you can explain, and keep the 610. Notice the median doesn't move at all, while the mean drops by almost 200 ms. When you can't defend removing extreme values, the median is the safer summary.

#Exercise 6: A gradebook that's too wide

Reshape the gradebook so each row is one student's score on one quiz. Then print the average score per quiz and per student, and plot each student's scores across the three quizzes.

Need a hint?

grades.melt(id_vars="student", var_name="quiz", value_name="score"). For the chart, long.pivot(index="quiz", columns="student", values="score") gives one column per student, which plot() draws as one line each.

Show solution

In the long table, "quiz" is a real column, so one groupby answers each question, with no code that names quiz1, quiz2, quiz3 one by one. Add a quiz4 column to grades and every line above still works unchanged.

#Challenge: Clean an animal-shelter log

Write clean_shelter(raw) that returns a clean DataFrame with columns animal_id, species, age_years, days_in_shelter, and adopted (a real bool). Ages like 6 months become 0.5; ? is missing; a negative stay is impossible; repeated rows go. Then compare the average stay by species before and after cleaning.

Need a hint?

Work column by column. For ages, mark which entries end in months, strip the word, convert to numbers, and divide those by 12. For adopted, normalize case and map {"yes": True, "y": True, "no": False, "n": False}. Keep 400 days: a long stay is unusual, not impossible.

Show solution

Before cleaning, dogs are split across Dog, DOG, dog and dog, and the DOG group's average is −3 days, the impossible stay counted twice. After cleaning there are three species, and the count column shows each average's real basis. Cats average a long stay because of one 400-day resident. That's a real animal, and the right response is to report the median too, not to delete the cat. (The .astype(bool) at the end is safe here only because every answer mapped; check for unmapped values before forcing a type.)

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why one outlier moves the mean but barely touches the median.
  • Measure spread with standard deviation and the interquartile range (IQR).
  • Draw and read a histogram, and see how the number of bins changes the story.
  • Read a box plot, and name what it can hide.
  • Choose a bar, line, scatter, or distribution chart from the question being asked.

Two pizza shops near you both advertise "average delivery: 30 minutes." Your party starts in 35 minutes. Which one do you call?

If averages told the whole story, it wouldn't matter. It matters a lot. One shop delivers in 28 to 32 minutes almost every time. The other usually arrives in about 20 minutes, but a third of its orders come from a kitchen across town and take closer to 50. Same average, very different chance of cold guests. This lesson is about the numbers and charts that tell those two shops apart.

#Mean and median react differently to one bad night

The mean adds every value and divides by how many there are. The median sorts the values and takes the middle one (or the average of the two middle ones). Here are nine ordinary deliveries, and then the same nine plus one driver who got lost:

One value out of ten dragged the mean up by more than six minutes. The median didn't move, because sorting puts 95 at the end and the middle stays where it was. Step through the hand calculation and watch where 95 ends up:

The mean is 42.6 minutes, which is longer than four of the five deliveries. That's the rule of thumb: when data is skewed (a long tail on one side) or has outliers, report the median, or report both and say why they differ. Incomes, house prices, and wait times are usually skewed.

#Spread: how far values wander from the center

Two datasets can share a center and still be nothing alike. Spread measures how far values sit from the middle. Let's build a month of deliveries for both shops. Crust Club sends 140 orders from its nearby kitchen and 60 from the far one:

Read across the rows. The means are within half a minute of each other, but almost everything else differs:

  • Standard deviation (std) is roughly the typical distance from the mean. About 2 minutes for Slice House, more than 12 for Crust Club.
  • IQR is the width of the middle half of the data: the 75th percentile minus the 25th. It ignores the top and bottom quarters, so a few wild values can't inflate it the way they inflate the standard deviation.
  • The last column answers the question you actually care about. Slice House makes it within 35 minutes nearly every time; Crust Club, about 70% of the time.

deliveries.groupby("shop")["minutes"].describe() prints count, mean, std, min, quartiles, and max in one call. It's usually the first summary to run on a numeric column.

⚠️ Watch out

pandas and NumPy disagree about standard deviation. pd.Series([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]).std() gives 2.138, but np.std([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]) gives 2.0. pandas divides by n − 1 (the sample standard deviation, ddof=1), and NumPy divides by n (ddof=0). Neither is wrong. Pick one, pass ddof= explicitly when you mix libraries, and say which you used.

#Histograms show the shape the summary hides

A histogram splits the number line into equal bins and draws a bar for how many values land in each. Stack the two shops on the same x-axis so their shapes line up:

Crust Club is bimodal: two humps, one per kitchen. Its mean lands in the valley between them, so a "typical" 30-minute Crust Club delivery barely exists. When a mean falls where there's almost no data, it's describing nobody.

The bin count is a choice, and it changes what you see. Here is the same Crust Club column three ways:

Matplotlib's default is 10 bins, whatever the data. Try a few counts before you trust a shape, and use the same bin edges when you compare groups.

#Box plots: five numbers in one picture

A box plot draws the five-number summary. The box runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile (so its width is the IQR), the line inside is the median, and the whiskers reach the furthest points within 1.5 × IQR of the box. Anything beyond the whiskers is drawn as a separate dot. seaborn draws one per group from a DataFrame:

Box plots are compact, so they shine when you compare many groups side by side. Their blind spot is shape: Crust Club's box is wide, but nothing about a box says "two humps." That's why the dots are layered on top. With a few hundred points or fewer, show the points; with thousands, pair the box plot with a histogram.

#Let the question pick the chart

Charts aren't decoration. Each form answers one kind of question well:

Here is the delivery data answering four different questions:

Two rules travel with these forms. Bars encode amounts by length, so the axis must start at zero, or a bar twice as tall won't mean twice as much. A line implies the points are connected in order, so only use one when the x-axis has a real order like time; a line across shop names suggests a trend between them that doesn't exist.

🧪 Try it yourself

In the four-chart cell, change axes[0, 1].set_ylim(0, 40) to axes[0, 1].set_ylim(29, 30.6) and run it. The same flat wobble now looks like a dramatic rollercoaster. You'll take that trick apart in the next lesson.

⚠️ Watch out

Reporting a mean for bimodal or skewed data. "Crust Club averages 29.5 minutes" is true and useless. If a histogram shows two humps, describe the groups separately ("about 70% of orders arrive in roughly 20 minutes; the rest take closer to 50"). If it shows a long tail, lead with the median.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You add one delivery of 300 minutes to a column of 200 deliveries that each took about 30 minutes. What happens?

  • Backwards. Sorting puts 300 at the end, so the middle value hardly moves.

  • The mean shares the extra 270 minutes across 201 deliveries (about 1.3 minutes each), while the middle of the sorted list stays put.

  • Only the mean uses the size of every value. The median only cares about order.

Show answer

B. The mean shares the extra 270 minutes across 201 deliveries (about 1.3 minutes each), while the middle of the sorted list stays put.

2Crust Club's box plot shows a wide box from 21 to 41 minutes. What can't you learn from the box alone?

  • That's exactly what the box shows: the 25th to 75th percentile.

  • The line inside the box is the median.

  • A box summarizes with five numbers, and two humps or one wide hump give similar boxes. A histogram or the raw points reveal the shape.

Show answer

C. A box summarizes with five numbers, and two humps or one wide hump give similar boxes. A histogram or the raw points reveal the shape.

3A café owner asks, "Did our average wait time change over the last 12 months?" Which chart fits best?

  • Months have a real order, and a line shows change from one to the next.

  • A histogram pools the year together and loses the order of the months, which is the whole question.

  • Names have no order and no meaning as numbers, so the pattern would be noise.

Show answer

A. Months have a real order, and a line shows change from one to the next.

4np.std(data) prints 4.47 but data_series.std() prints 4.71 for the same numbers. Why?

  • Both are computed correctly; they use different formulas.

  • pandas defaults to the sample standard deviation (ddof=1). Pass ddof=1 to NumPy, or ddof=0 to pandas, to make them match.

  • pandas skips missing values (NaN), not large ones.

Show answer

B. pandas defaults to the sample standard deviation (ddof=1). Pass ddof=1 to NumPy, or ddof=0 to pandas, to make them match.

Key takeaways

  • The mean feels every value, so outliers and long tails pull it. The median only cares about order.
  • Report spread with the center: standard deviation for roughly symmetric data, IQR when there are outliers.
  • A histogram shows shape, including two humps that summary numbers hide. Try more than one bin count.
  • A box plot compares groups compactly but hides shape, so layer the points or add a histogram.
  • Pick the chart from the question: bars for amounts (from zero), lines for ordered time, scatter for two numbers, histogram or box for one number's spread.

#Further reading

  • pandas DataFrame.describe (opens in a new tab): what each row of the summary means, plus the percentiles= option.
  • Fundamentals of Data Visualization: histograms and density plots (opens in a new tab): Claus Wilke's free book shows how bin width and density smoothing can each mislead.
  • Matplotlib Axes.hist (opens in a new tab): every option for bins, ranges, and stacked or step histograms.

What you'll learn

  • Measure how much a truncated axis exaggerates a difference, using the lie factor.
  • Rebuild a bar chart from a zero baseline with direct value labels.
  • Show individual data points so readers can see spread, not only averages.
  • Replace a dual-axis chart with one that puts both series on a common scale.
  • Write chart titles and labels that state the finding, with units, without relying on color alone.

The school newsletter just ran this chart under the headline "Tutoring sends scores soaring!" The tutored bar towers over the other one. Before reading on, guess: how much higher do you think the tutored group's average actually is?

The scores here are simulated with a fixed seed (default_rng(21)), so you get exactly the same 120 students every time you run it. By the end of this lesson you'll have replaced this chart with a two-panel figure that shows the real gap and every student behind it, and you'll have fixed a second, sneakier chart from the same newsletter.

#Step 1: Check the claim with numbers first

A chart is a claim about numbers, so start with the numbers. agg computes several summaries per group in one call:

The tutored group's mean is 2.8 points higher. Meanwhile each group's scores spread about 9 or 10 points either side of its mean, and each group spans more than 40 points from its lowest score to its highest. The gap is real in this sample, but it is small compared with how much students differ from each other. Whether it's worth a headline is a separate question, and one the chart answered dishonestly.

#Step 2: Measure how much the chart exaggerates

Edward Tufte, who wrote some of the most influential books on statistical graphics, proposed a number for this: the lie factor, the size of the effect shown in the graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data. A truthful chart scores 1.

Bars encode a number by their length. Cutting off the bottom 72 points of both bars leaves only the tips, and the tips differ by a huge ratio even though the totals don't. With the axis at zero, the lie factor drops to exactly 1, because the drawn lengths are proportional to the values again.

#Step 3: Rebuild the bars from zero, with labels

Three changes: start at zero, print the value on each bar so nobody has to squint at gridlines, and write a title that states what the chart shows (computed from the data, so it can't drift out of date).

Now the bars look nearly equal, because they nearly are. Notice that the honest version is less exciting. That's the point: the exciting version was manufactured by the axis, not found in the data.

⚠️ Watch out

"Start at zero" is a rule for bars, not for every chart. A line chart encodes values by position and slope, not length, so a temperature line from 18 to 24 °C is fine. But a line's range still makes a claim: zoom in far enough and noise looks like a crisis. Pick a range that matches a change that would matter, and label the axis so readers can see what you chose.

#Step 4: Show every student, not just two averages

Two bars hide the most important fact: how much the groups overlap. A strip plot draws one dot per student, jittered up and down so they don't sit on top of each other. A short black tick marks each mean.

More than a third of tutored students scored below the other group's average. This chart would stop any reader from concluding that tutoring transforms everyone's grades, and it does it without a single extra word. (Whether tutoring caused even the 2.8-point gap is a different question. Students chose to sign up, and Module 6 is about why that matters.)

#Step 5: Replace the dual-axis chart

Page two of the newsletter had this one. It plots two different measures, each with its own y-axis:

The lines hug each other, which looks like strong evidence. It isn't evidence of anything: whoever makes the chart picks both axis ranges independently, so any two rising series can be stretched to overlap. Change set_ylim(70.8, 74.1) to set_ylim(0, 100) and the purple line goes flat.

The fix is to put both series on one shared, meaningful scale. Here that's percent change since September:

Two other honest fixes work too: two separate panels stacked with a shared x-axis, or a scatter plot of one measure against the other. And even with an honest chart, two things that both rise across a school year don't show that one drives the other. Scores often climb as the year goes on anyway.

#Step 6: Make color and labels carry their weight

Look back at the newsletter's choices: red for "our" group and gray for the other, a shouting title, no units. Each of the rebuilt charts follows a few rules you can apply to any figure:

Choice Rule Why
Color One color per group, the same in every chart Readers learn "blue = tutored" once
Palette Blue and orange, not red and green About 1 in 12 men has some color vision deficiency, usually red-green
Labels Name lines and bars directly, not only in a legend Identity never depends on color alone
Title State the finding, computed from the data The reader knows what to look for, and it stays correct
Axes Name the measure and its unit "Score (out of 100)" beats "score"

Combine Steps 3 and 4 into one figure, with a figure-level title that summarizes both panels.

#The finished program

This cell is self-contained: it rebuilds the data and the final figure from scratch, which is how you'd keep it in a real notebook.

The function takes the column names, group order, colors, and unit as arguments, so the same honest layout works for any two-group comparison: sleep hours by grade, commute minutes by bus route, or anything you meet in the capstone.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Step 2, why did the lie factor fall to exactly 1 when the axis started at 0?

  • With a zero baseline, a bar for 76.5 is 76.5 units long, and the ratio of lengths equals the ratio of means.

  • The means are unchanged; only how much of each bar is drawn changes.

  • It returned 44 for the same gap with the axis at 72. The baseline is what changed.

Show answer

A. With a zero baseline, a bar for 76.5 is 76.5 units long, and the ratio of lengths equals the ratio of means.

2Why did Step 4 add a strip plot instead of error bars or a bigger title?

  • No such rule. The strip plot answers a different question than the bars do.

  • Seeing that more than a third of tutored students fall below the other group's mean keeps readers from imagining that every tutored student did better.

  • It can (sns.barplot). We used matplotlib for the bars because it's simpler to label.

Show answer

B. Seeing that more than a third of tutored students fall below the other group's mean keeps readers from imagining that every tutored student did better.

3A teammate fixes the dual-axis chart by setting both y-axes to start at zero. What's still wrong?

  • The two axes still have different units and ranges chosen independently, so how the lines line up is still the chart maker's choice.

  • The fix is one shared scale (like percent change), separate panels, or a scatter plot of one measure against the other.

  • Lines can start at zero or not. The problem here is having two independent y-axes.

Show answer

B. The fix is one shared scale (like percent change), separate panels, or a scatter plot of one measure against the other.

Key takeaways

  • Check the numbers before you trust the picture. A big-looking gap can be small next to the spread within each group.
  • Bars encode length, so they start at zero. The lie factor measures how far a chart strays from that.
  • Show the data points (or a distribution) next to averages so readers can see the overlap.
  • Dual axes let the chart maker line up any two series. Use one shared scale, separate panels, or a scatter plot.
  • Keep one color per group across every chart, label things directly, put units on axes, and compute titles from the data.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a third panel to honest_comparison: overlaid histograms of the two groups with shared bin edges.
  • Write a function check_bar_axis(ax) that warns when a bar chart's y-axis doesn't start at zero. (Hint: ax.get_ylim() returns the axis range.)
  • Pass honest_comparison a different dataset, such as the two pizza shops from the Notes lesson, and adjust the y-limit for minutes instead of a 100-point score.
  • Have the function also return a one-sentence alt text built from the same numbers as the title.

#Further reading

  • Fundamentals of Data Visualization: the principle of proportional ink (opens in a new tab): why bars must start at zero, and the cases where other charts may not.
  • Why not to use two axes, and what to use instead (opens in a new tab): Datawrapper's guide to every alternative to a dual-axis chart, with examples.
  • Matplotlib Axes.bar_label (opens in a new tab): formatting and placing value labels on bars.

What you'll learn

  • Pick the right center and spread for skewed and symmetric data.
  • Use histograms and box plots to describe shape, spread, and outliers.
  • Match a question to the chart that answers it.
  • Repair charts that exaggerate with their axis or depend on color alone.

Run this setup cell first. Every exercise below uses it, and the fixed seed means your numbers will match the sample output.

#Warm-up

Six friends report their weekly allowance in dollars. One of them works weekends at a car wash. Predict the mean and the median before you run this.

The mean says the "typical" friend gets $42.50, which is true of nobody in the group. The median, $11, is what five of the six would recognize.

#Exercise 1: Report the right center for sleep data

A health class surveyed 80 ninth graders and 80 twelfth graders about last night's sleep. Some twelfth graders had pulled near all-nighters before an exam.

Print the mean, median, standard deviation, and IQR of hours for each grade in one table. Then decide which center you'd report for twelfth graders, and why.

Sample output (your table should have these columns):

Need a hint?

groupby("grade")["hours"].agg([...]) accepts strings like "mean" and also your own functions. Write a small iqr(s) function that returns s.quantile(0.75) - s.quantile(0.25).

Show solution

For twelfth graders the ten short nights drag the mean down and inflate the standard deviation, while the median and IQR barely notice them. Report the median (and the IQR), and mention the short nights separately: "Most seniors slept about 7 hours; 10 of 80 slept under 5."

#Exercise 2: Find the two groups in commute times

Here are commute times, in minutes, for 200 students. Some walk; some ride a bus with a long route.

Draw the histogram twice, side by side: once with bins=4 and once with bins=np.arange(0, 56, 2). Describe the shape you see in the second one, and estimate how many students are in each group by counting commutes under 20 minutes.

Sample output: two histograms, plus one printed line like Under 20 min: ___ students, 20 min or more: ___ students.

Need a hint?

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3)) gives you two axes. For the count, (commute < 20).sum() counts the True values.

Show solution

The narrow bins show a bimodal shape: walkers around 9 minutes and bus riders around 34. With 4 bins the gap between them is swallowed. Any single average of this column describes neither group well.

#Exercise 3: Compare four grades with box plots

Draw horizontal box plots of daily screen-time hours for the four grades, in grade order. Then print each grade's IQR and the number of points beyond the whiskers (more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile). Which grade varies the most?

Sample output: four box plots and a small table with columns iqr and outliers.

Need a hint?

Pass order=["9th", "10th", "11th", "12th"] to sns.boxplot. For outliers, write a function that computes q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1) for a Series and counts the values above it, then use it in .agg.

Show solution

Eleventh grade has the largest IQR, about 3.4 hours, so its middle half is the most spread out, and it's the only grade with outliers. Outlier dots are worth a second look (a 12-hour day might be a typo), but they're not automatically errors. Never delete one just because the plot drew it as a dot.

#Exercise 4: Match each question to a chart

For each question, name the chart you'd use: bar, line, scatter, or histogram.

  1. Did library visits change across the school year?
  2. Which of five clubs raised the most money?
  3. Do students who sleep more tend to have higher grades?
  4. How long do most students spend on homework each night?

Then draw the chart for question 1 using this data, with labeled axes and a title that states what you see.

Need a hint?

Ask what the x-axis would be. Months have an order, clubs don't, and two numeric measures per student call for one dot per student.

Show solution

1 is a line (ordered time), 2 a bar (amounts across categories, from zero), 3 a scatter (two numbers per student), and 4 a histogram (one number's distribution).

The y-axis starts at zero here because the dips are big enough to see anyway. For a line that wasn't required, but it keeps the January dip in proportion.

#Exercise 5: Repair the bake-sale chart

First, compute the lie factor comparing the 10th and 11th grade bars. Then redraw the chart with a zero baseline, dollar labels on each bar, a y-axis label, and a title that states the actual finding.

Sample output: a line like Lie factor: __, and the repaired chart.

Need a hint?

The lie factor is (effect shown) ÷ (effect in the data). The shown effect is (431 - 390) / (398 - 390) - 1; the real effect is 431 / 398 - 1. ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="$%d") adds dollar labels.

Show solution

A lie factor near 50 means the original chart made the gap look about fifty times bigger, in relative terms, than it was. The title is computed from the data, so it stays correct if a late donation arrives.

#Exercise 6: Make a chart readable without color

This chart works only if you can tell red from green, and only after hunting through a legend.

Redraw it with blue and orange, a label at the end of each line instead of a legend, axis labels, and a title that states the finding. Then build and print an alt-text sentence from the data (so it would update if the numbers changed).

Need a hint?

Loop over [("Robotics", BLUE), ("Drama", ORANGE)]. To label the end of a line, ax.annotate(name, (len(months) - 1, last_value), xytext=(6, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center").

Show solution

With the names on the lines, a reader who sees no color at all can still read the chart. The markers help too: a printout in grayscale still shows where each month's value is.

#Challenge: Four datasets, one set of statistics

In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe published four small datasets to make a point. Type them in, then for each set print the mean of x, mean of y, standard deviation of y, and the correlation between x and y. Finally, draw all four as scatter plots in a 2×2 grid with the best-fit line on each.

Need a hint?

np.corrcoef(xs, ys)[0, 1] gives the correlation. slope, intercept = np.polyfit(xs, ys, 1) gives the best-fit line. plt.subplots(2, 2, sharex=True, sharey=True) keeps the four panels comparable.

Show solution

Every row of the table matches to two decimal places, and every set gets the same line (y ≈ 3 + 0.5x). The pictures disagree completely: only set I looks like the "moderate linear relationship" the numbers describe. Summaries compress; charts show what got compressed away. Draw the data before you trust a statistic.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read a correlation coefficient, and name two things it can't detect.
  • List the explanations for a correlation besides "X causes Y."
  • Use a simulation to show how a confounder creates a correlation, and remove it.
  • Explain why a huge biased sample can be worse than a small random one.
  • Recognize survivorship bias, and write a claim limited to what the data supports.

In 2012 the New England Journal of Medicine published a short paper by the cardiologist Franz Messerli with a startling chart. Across 23 countries, the more chocolate people ate per person, the more Nobel Prizes the country had won per person. The correlation was r = 0.79, which is very strong.

Messerli himself called the result "hypothesis-generating only." But news sites ran headlines like "Eating chocolate produces Nobel prize winners." Nobody had measured whether any laureate ate chocolate. The data were country averages, and rich countries both buy more chocolate and fund more research. This lesson gives you the tools to see through a claim like that in about thirty seconds.

#What r measures, and what it misses

The Pearson correlation coefficient, r, measures how closely two numeric variables follow a straight line. It runs from −1 (a perfect downhill line) through 0 (no straight-line pattern) to +1 (a perfect uphill line). Here are five datasets of 150 points each:

The last panel is the warning. y depends completely on x, yet r is about zero, because the pattern is a curve, not a line: the left half slopes down and the right half slopes up, and they cancel. r near 0 means "no straight-line relationship," not "no relationship." And r says nothing about why two things move together, which is the bigger problem.

#Four reasons two variables move together

When you see a correlation between X and Y, there are four broad explanations, and "X causes Y" is only one of them:

  1. X causes Y. Studying more raises test scores.
  2. Y causes X (reverse causation). Messerli himself noted that smarter populations might buy more chocolate, rather than the other way round.
  3. Something else causes both (a confounder). National wealth plausibly raises both chocolate sales and research funding.
  4. Chance. Compare enough variables and some will line up by luck. Per capita cheese consumption once tracked deaths by bedsheet entanglement remarkably closely.

#Watch a confounder build a fake relationship

Simulation lets you know the truth for certain, because you wrote it. Here, temperature drives both ice cream and sunscreen sales at a beach shop, and neither one affects the other at all:

DataFrame.corr() gives r for every pair of columns. Ice cream and sunscreen correlate at 0.63, and someone looking at only those two columns might start a "sunscreen promotes snacking" theory.

To check, hold the confounder still. One way is to remove the part of each variable that temperature explains (fit a line against temperature with np.polyfit, then keep the leftovers, called residuals) and correlate what's left:

On the left, darker dots (hotter days) sit in the top right: the whole pattern is temperature. On the right, once temperature is accounted for, a day with surprisingly high ice cream sales tells you nothing about sunscreen. In real data you rarely know every confounder, which is why careful researchers prefer randomized experiments: flipping a coin to decide who gets the treatment breaks every hidden link at once.

⚠️ Watch out

"Controlled for X" only covers X. Removing temperature fixed this simulation because temperature was the only confounder. With real data there may be others you never measured. Write "after accounting for temperature, the correlation disappeared," not "we proved ice cream and sunscreen are unrelated."

#A bigger sample won't fix a biased one

In 1936 the Literary Digest magazine polled ten million Americans about the presidential election, mostly drawn from its own readers, car registrations, and telephone directories. About 2.4 million replied. It predicted Alf Landon would win 57% of the vote. Franklin Roosevelt won about 61% and carried every state except Maine and Vermont.

In 1936, people with cars and phones were wealthier than average and leaned toward Landon, and the people who bothered to mail back a ballot leaned even further. Here's a simulation of the first problem. A quarter of voters are on the lists, and they favor Roosevelt far less than everyone else:

The random sample of 1,000 lands within a few points of the truth. The list-only sample of 20,000 is off by more than 20 points, and polling 200,000 from the same lists would land in the same wrong place. Sample size shrinks random error; it does nothing about bias. Ask who could end up in the data, and who couldn't.

#Survivorship bias: the data that didn't come back

During World War II, the statistician Abraham Wald worked with the US military on where to add armor to bombers. Returning planes were full of bullet holes in the wings and body, and the obvious plan was to armor those spots. Wald's point was that these were the planes that survived. Planes hit in the engines mostly didn't return to be counted, so the places with no holes were the ones that needed armor.

The same trap shows up everywhere data gets filtered by an outcome: studying only successful startups to learn what makes startups succeed, averaging the scores of students who chose to submit them to a test-optional college, or judging old buildings by the ones still standing. Before analyzing, ask what process decided which rows made it into your file.

#When splitting the data flips the answer

The strangest trap gets the whole next lesson. In Simpson's paradox, a trend that holds in every subgroup reverses when the groups are combined, because a confounder is spread unevenly across them. You'll rebuild the famous real case, UC Berkeley's 1973 graduate admissions.

#Writing a claim that fits the data

Each of these traps has the same cure: say exactly what the data shows, and no more. A useful template:

In [who and when], [X] and [Y] were [direction] related (r = …). This doesn't show that X causes Y; [confounder] could explain both. Because the data came from [sample], it may not hold for [other people].

Compare "Chocolate makes nations smarter" with "Across 23 countries, chocolate consumption per person and Nobel laureates per person were strongly correlated (r = 0.79). National wealth could explain both, and country averages say nothing about individual chocolate eaters." The second is less exciting and much more likely to be true.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1In a study of 200 students, the correlation between hours of sleep and reaction time is r = 0.02. What can you conclude?

  • r only detects straight-line patterns. A curve (too little and too much sleep both slow you down) could give r near 0.

  • That's all r = 0.02 tells you. A scatter plot would show whether there's a curved pattern r can't see.

  • r is nearly zero, and even a large r wouldn't establish cause.

Show answer

B. That's all r = 0.02 tells you. A scatter plot would show whether there's a curved pattern r can't see.

2A city finds that neighborhoods with more libraries have lower crime rates. Which is a confounder that could explain both?

  • A confounder causes both variables. Wealthier areas may have more libraries and less crime for separate reasons.

  • That's a consequence of having libraries, not a common cause of libraries and crime.

  • That doesn't plausibly cause both how many libraries exist and how much crime there is.

Show answer

A. A confounder causes both variables. Wealthier areas may have more libraries and less crime for separate reasons.

3An online poll gets 50,000 votes on whether school should start later; 85% say yes. A random survey of 800 students finds 61%. Which should you trust more?

  • Size reduces random error, not bias. People who feel strongly are far more likely to click on an online poll.

  • A random sample of 800 is usually within a few points of the truth. The online poll's error comes from who chose to answer, and more votes don't fix that.

Show answer

B. A random sample of 800 is usually within a few points of the truth. The online poll's error comes from who chose to answer, and more votes don't fix that.

4A study of famous entrepreneurs finds most of them took big risks early. Why is "taking big risks leads to success" a weak conclusion?

  • Even a large sample of famous entrepreneurs would have the same problem.

  • That's survivorship bias. You'd need to know what happened to everyone who took big risks, not just the winners.

  • Possibly, but the main flaw is who got counted at all.

Show answer

B. That's survivorship bias. You'd need to know what happened to everyone who took big risks, not just the winners.

Key takeaways

  • r measures straight-line association from −1 to 1. It misses curves and says nothing about cause.
  • A correlation can come from X causing Y, Y causing X, a confounder causing both, or chance.
  • Removing a confounder's effect can make a correlation vanish, but only for the confounders you measured.
  • Bias doesn't shrink with sample size. A small random sample beats a huge biased one.
  • Ask what decided which rows made it into your data. Survivors, volunteers, and responders differ from everyone else.
  • Write claims that name the sample, the strength, and the alternative explanations.

#Further reading

  • Spurious Correlations (opens in a new tab): Tyler Vigen's collection of real datasets that line up by pure chance, with r values.
  • Statistics Done Wrong (opens in a new tab): Alex Reinhart's free, readable guide to the mistakes researchers make, including confounding and biased samples.
  • pandas DataFrame.corr (opens in a new tab): computing correlation tables, including the rank-based method="spearman" for relationships that always rise (or always fall) but not along a straight line.

What you'll learn

  • Enter a real dataset in tidy (long) form and check it against published totals.
  • Compute pooled rates and per-group rates with groupby and pivot.
  • Find the lurking variable by charting who applied where.
  • Explain the paradox as a weighted average, and compute a rate standardized to the same mix of departments.
  • Write a conclusion that says what the data shows and what it can't.

In the fall of 1973, the University of California, Berkeley admitted about 44% of the men who applied to its graduate programs and about 35% of the women. With more than 12,000 applicants, a gap that big looks hard to explain away, and it raised an obvious question: were departments treating women unfairly?

The statistician Peter Bickel and two colleagues looked closer, and in 1975 they published a now-famous analysis in Science. Department by department, the gap didn't hold up. You're going to rebuild their argument using the real numbers for Berkeley's six largest departments, which the paper identified only by letter. The question to keep in mind is which of these two paths explains the gap:

#Step 1: Enter the data in tidy form

Each row is one gender in one department, with counts, not percentages. Counts let you recompute any rate later; percentages alone would make it impossible to combine departments correctly.

The assert is a cheap guard against typos: if any count were mistyped, the total wouldn't match the 4,526 applicants in the published table, and the notebook would stop right here instead of producing a wrong chart later.

#Step 2: Compute the pooled rates

"Pooled" means you add up the counts across all departments first, then divide. That's what the headline number did.

In these six departments the gap is even wider than in the university as a whole: 44.5% against 30.4%. If you stopped here, you'd conclude that these departments favored men.

#Step 3: Look department by department

pivot reshapes the tidy table so each department is a row and each gender a column, which makes the comparison easy to read and to plot.

The direction flips. Women's admission rate was higher in A, B, D, and F, and lower in C and E by three or four points. In department A, women were admitted 82% of the time against 62% for men. Every department's numbers are real, and so is the pooled gap. Both can be true at once, and the next step shows how.

#Step 4: Find the lurking variable

Look at where each group applied. Two numbers per department tell the story: how selective it is (its admission rate for everyone) and what share of its applicants were women.

Departments A and B admitted almost two-thirds of applicants, and only a small share of their applicants were women. Departments C through F admitted far fewer people, and that's where most women applied. Department is the lurking variable (a confounder from Module 6's Notes): it's linked to gender (who applied where) and to the outcome (how likely admission was).

#Step 5: See the flip as a weighted average

Here's the arithmetic behind the paradox. A group's pooled rate is the average of its department rates, weighted by where that group applied:

pooled rate = Σ (share of the group's applications to the department × the group's admission rate in that department)

Men's weights pile up on A and B, with their high rates. Women's weights pile up on C through F, with their low rates. So you can ask a fair question: what would women's pooled rate be if they had applied to departments in the same proportions as men?

The first line reproduces women's pooled 30.4%, which confirms the formula. The second is a standardized rate: women's own department-by-department success, applied to men's mix of applications. It comes out at 51.6%, higher than men's 44.5%. The gap in the headline came from where people applied, not from how each department treated the applicants in front of it.

⚠️ Watch out

Averaging percentages instead of counts. by_dept["Women"].mean() gives about 41.7%, which matches nothing: it treats department B's 25 women the same as department C's 593. Pool by summing counts, or weight each rate by its share of applicants, as above.

#Step 6: Write a claim the data supports

Here's a careful summary of what these numbers show, in the template from the Notes:

In fall 1973, across Berkeley's six largest graduate departments, men were admitted at 44.5% and women at 30.4%. Within departments, women's rates were higher in four of the six and slightly lower in two. The pooled gap is explained by women applying mostly to departments that admitted few applicants of either gender.

And here's what it does not show:

  • That no one was ever treated unfairly. These are counts, with no data on applicants' qualifications. A department could have treated individuals unfairly in either direction without it showing up in totals.
  • Why women applied to more selective departments. Bickel and his colleagues argued that the cause lay earlier, in which fields women had been steered toward before they ever applied. That's a question about a different stage of the pipeline, needing different data.
  • Anything about other years or universities. Six departments in one year are one snapshot.

#The finished program

This standalone cell rebuilds the data and the whole analysis, and prints a short report. Run it on a fresh runtime and you'll get the same numbers.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did Step 1 store applicant and admitted counts rather than just each department's admission percentage?

  • They can. The problem is combining them.

  • Pooling needs the totals. With only percentages, department B's 25 women would count as much as department C's 593.

  • It can, as berkeley["admitted"] / berkeley["applied"] shows.

Show answer

B. Pooling needs the totals. With only percentages, department B's 25 women would count as much as department C's 593.

2What did the standardized rate in Step 5 hold fixed?

  • It used women's own rates in each department, not the combined rates.

  • Using the same weights for both groups removes the effect of where people applied, leaving only how they fared within departments.

  • Totals don't change the rate; the weights (shares of applications) are what matter.

Show answer

B. Using the same weights for both groups removes the effect of where people applied, leaving only how they fared within departments.

3A friend reads your analysis and says, "So Berkeley proved there was no discrimination." What's the best reply?

  • The data has no information on applicants' qualifications, so it can't rule out unfair treatment of individuals.

  • That's the supported claim. It also leaves open why women applied mostly to the most selective departments.

  • The pooled gap is real, but the department breakdown shows it's explained by application patterns, not by departments' decisions.

Show answer

B. That's the supported claim. It also leaves open why women applied mostly to the most selective departments.

Key takeaways

  • Simpson's paradox: a trend in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are pooled, because the groups differ in size and in their baseline rates.
  • Keep counts, not just percentages, so you can pool and re-weight correctly.
  • A pooled rate is a weighted average of group rates. Different weights can flip the comparison.
  • A standardized rate puts both groups on the same mix, isolating the within-group difference.
  • The careful claim names what the data explains and what it leaves open.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Standardize the other way: compute men's pooled rate using women's mix of applications, and compare it with women's actual 30.4%.
  • Draw a "slope chart": one line per department connecting men's rate to women's rate, so the direction of each gap is visible at a glance.
  • Write a function pooled_vs_stratified(df, group, stratum, success, total) that prints both comparisons and flags when their directions disagree, then try it on the kidney stone data in the Practice lesson.

#Further reading

  • Simpson's paradox (Wikipedia) (opens in a new tab): the full Berkeley table, the kidney stone example, and the history of the idea.
  • Simpson's Paradox (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy) (opens in a new tab): a deeper look at why the paradox is really about causal structure, not arithmetic.
  • pandas DataFrame.pivot (opens in a new tab): reshaping tidy data into a comparison table, and when to use pivot_table instead.

What you'll learn

  • Compute and read a correlation matrix, then check the strongest pair with a scatter plot.
  • Stratify by a confounder and compare results within groups.
  • Correct a biased sample by reweighting to known population shares.
  • Measure how survivorship and pooling distort results, using simulated and real data.
  • Rewrite overconfident claims so they match the evidence.

Run the setup cell first. The seed keeps every simulated dataset identical to the ones in the solutions.

#Warm-up

Here y is completely determined by x. Predict r before you run it.

The values fall and then rise symmetrically, so the downhill half cancels the uphill half exactly. Perfect dependence, zero correlation.

#Exercise 1: Find the strongest relationship in a survey

Print the correlation matrix, then find the pair of different columns with the largest absolute correlation using code (not by eye). Draw that pair as a scatter plot with labeled axes and r in the title.

Sample output: the matrix, then a line like Strongest pair: ('phone_hours', 'sleep_hours') r = -0.77.

Need a hint?

survey.corr().unstack() turns the matrix into a Series indexed by pairs. Drop the self-pairs (where the value is exactly 1), take .abs(), and use .idxmax().

Show solution

Taking .abs() before idxmax matters: the strongest relationship here is negative, and without .abs() you'd pick the strongest positive pair instead. Each pair appears twice in the unstacked Series (A with B, and B with A), which is harmless here.

#Exercise 2: Does tutoring lower grades?

A different school's data seems to show that tutored students finish with lower scores. But students choose tutoring when they're struggling.

  1. Compare the mean final score of the two groups overall.
  2. Split students into prior-grade bands (under 65, 65–74, 75–84, 85+) and compare the groups within each band.
  3. Draw a grouped bar chart of the within-band means, and write one sentence on what explains the overall result.
Need a hint?

pd.cut(tutoring["prior_grade"], [0, 65, 75, 85, 101], labels=[...], right=False) makes the bands. Then pivot_table(index="band", columns="group", values="final", aggfunc="mean", observed=True) builds the comparison table.

Show solution

Overall, tutored students averaged about 8 points lower. Within each band they scored 2 to 5 points higher. Prior grade is the confounder: weaker students were much more likely to sign up, and weaker students score lower whether tutored or not. Notice the counts too: the under-65 band is mostly tutored students and the 85+ band has none, which is exactly the uneven mix that produces a reversal.

#Exercise 3: Fix a lopsided survey

The cafeteria survey was handed out at lunch, when ninth graders eat on campus far more than seniors. The school has 300 students in each grade.

In real life you only see sample. Compute its raw mean satisfaction. Then compute a reweighted mean: each grade's sample mean, weighted by that grade's share of the whole school (25% each). Compare both with the true school mean, which you can see here only because the data is simulated.

Sample output: three lines, raw sample mean, reweighted mean, and true school mean.

Need a hint?

sample.groupby("grade")["satisfaction"].mean() gives one mean per grade. Multiply it by a Series of population shares (school["grade"].value_counts(normalize=True)) and .sum() the result.

Show solution

Half the responses came from ninth graders, the happiest group, so the raw mean overstates satisfaction by more than half a point. Reweighting gives each grade the voice its size deserves and lands close to the truth. This only fixes bias you can see: if the unhappy seniors who did answer differ from the ones who didn't, no weighting by grade can repair that.

#Exercise 4: Measure survivorship bias in investment funds

An advertisement says, "The average fund in our family returned 6.6% a year over five years!" Funds that lose money get closed, and closed funds disappear from the list.

Each row is one fund's yearly returns; a fund closes if its value ever drops below 85% of where it started. Print how many funds closed, the average yearly return of all 1,000 funds, and the average of the survivors only. Then draw two histograms (all funds, survivors) on the same bins.

Need a hint?

returns.mean(axis=1) gives each fund's average yearly return. Use closed as a mask: fund_avg[~closed] keeps the survivors.

Show solution

Every fund was drawn from the same distribution with a true average of 5%, so no fund was "skilled." Yet the survivors average about 6.6% because the unlucky ones were removed. The advertisement's number is true and still misleading.

#Exercise 5: Choose a kidney stone treatment

These are real results from a 1986 study comparing open surgery (A) with a less invasive procedure, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (B). Each row is successes out of patients treated.

Compute each treatment's pooled success rate and its rate for each stone size. Which treatment would you recommend for a patient with a small stone? With a large one? Draw a chart that makes your recommendation obvious.

Need a hint?

This is the same structure as the Berkeley data: group, stratum, successes, and totals. Pool by summing counts before dividing. Then look at how many small and large stones each treatment received.

Show solution

Recommend A for both sizes: it's better for small stones (93% vs 87%) and for large stones (73% vs 69%). B only looks better pooled because doctors gave B mostly to small stones, which are easier to treat, and A mostly to large ones. Stone size is the lurking variable, playing the role that department played at Berkeley.

#Exercise 6: Rewrite three overclaims

Rewrite each claim so it matches what the evidence can support. Name the sample, describe the strength, and give at least one alternative explanation or limit.

  1. "A survey of 400 students at our school found that breakfast eaters have higher grades (r = 0.3). Breakfast makes you smarter."
  2. "Our app makes people happy: 92% of users who answered our in-app survey gave it five stars."
  3. "Schools with more computers per student have higher test scores, so buying computers will raise scores."
Need a hint?

For each one, ask the four questions from the Notes: could it be reverse causation, a confounder, chance, or a sample that only includes certain people?

Show solution
  1. "Among 400 students at one school, those who ate breakfast had somewhat higher grades (r = 0.3, a modest correlation). This doesn't show breakfast causes higher grades: family routines, sleep, or income could affect both. It may not hold at other schools."
  2. "Of the users who chose to answer an in-app survey, 92% gave five stars. People who stopped using the app never saw the survey, and happy users may be more likely to answer, so this likely overstates satisfaction among everyone who tried it."
  3. "Schools with more computers per student tended to have higher test scores. Wealthier districts can afford both more computers and other advantages, so this doesn't show that adding computers would raise scores. An experiment that randomly assigns computers to schools could test that."

#Challenge: Build your own Simpson's paradox

Write a function simpson_check(df, group, stratum, success, total) that prints each group's pooled rate and per-stratum rates, and returns True when the group that wins pooled is not the group that wins in most strata. Test it on stones. Then invent a dataset of your own (two teaching methods in two schools, say) where Method X has the higher pass rate in both schools but the lower pass rate overall, and confirm your function returns True.

Need a hint?

The reversal needs two things: one school is much easier than the other, and the two methods are used in very different proportions in the two schools. Try making Method X common in the hard school and rare in the easy one.

Show solution

In the made-up data, X passes 90% vs 80% at the easy school and 30% vs 20% at the hard school, but 100 of X's 110 students are at the hard school, so X's pooled rate is only 35.5%, while Y's is 74.5%. A reversal always needs that combination: a stratum that strongly affects the outcome, and groups spread across the strata in very different proportions.

What you'll learn

  • Explain hidden state, and why a notebook can work for you and fail for everyone else.
  • Write cells that give the same result however many times you run them.
  • Make random sampling repeatable with seeds, and know what a seed can't fix.
  • Check a notebook with Restart session and run all before sharing it.
  • Record versions, parameters, and data checks inside the notebook itself.

Maya's notebook says the school's average reading time is 31.4 minutes a day, and her chart is already in the student newspaper. Her editor opens the notebook, chooses Run all, and gets this:

Two days ago Maya renamed the cell that created reading_clean, then deleted the old version. Her own session still had reading_clean in memory, so everything kept working for her. Nobody else can produce that 31.4, including Maya after her runtime resets. A result that only exists in one person's session isn't really a result.

#Notebook memory outlives your cells

A notebook is two things that can drift apart: the cells you see on the page, and the runtime's memory, which holds every variable any cell has ever created. Running a cell changes memory. Editing or deleting a cell doesn't. Three habits make them drift:

  • Deleting or renaming a cell whose variables are still in memory (Maya's problem).
  • Running cells out of order, such as cell 5, then cell 2, then cell 5 again. The bracketed counter beside each cell shows the order cells last ran, and the page doesn't show what memory looked like in between.
  • Running a cell twice when it changes something in place. Watch what happens when the "apply discount" cell gets run a second time to double-check its output:

The discount was applied twice, and nothing on the page says so. The fix is a rule: never overwrite your raw data; derive new names from it. member_prices = [round(p * 0.9, 2) for p in prices] gives the same answer on the first run and the fiftieth. In pandas, that means clean = raw[...].copy() and new columns on clean, rather than editing raw.

#Seeds make randomness repeatable

Random sampling, shuffling, and simulated data all draw from a random number generator. Give the generator a seed (any whole number) and it produces the same sequence every time:

Without a seed, np.random.default_rng() starts from fresh randomness every run, and df.sample(3) picks different rows every time. Seed every source of randomness you use: np.random.default_rng(seed) for NumPy, random_state= for DataFrame.sample and scikit-learn.

A seed makes a result repeatable, not right. Here, 20 classmates each draw a random sample of 40 students from the same school of 1,000 and report the average. Each uses a different seed:

Anyone who reruns seed 11 gets exactly the same answer, and it's still more than five minutes too high. The seed picked one sample out of many possible ones. Report how much results vary (rerun with several seeds, or give a range), and never try seeds until one gives the answer you hoped for.

⚠️ Watch out

Seed shopping. Running with seed 1, 2, 3… and keeping the one where your effect looks biggest is a quiet form of cheating, and the seed in your notebook makes it look reproducible. Choose the seed before you look at results, write it in your setup cell, and leave it alone.

#The test: Restart session and run all

The only way to prove a notebook doesn't depend on hidden state is to wipe memory and run it top to bottom. In Colab, use Runtime › Restart session and run all (some older guides call it Restart runtime, or Restart and run all). Or do it in two steps: Runtime › Restart session, then Runtime › Run all.

Do this before you share a notebook, before you copy a number into a report, and whenever something seems off. If it passes, three things are true:

  1. Every cell runs without an error, in page order.
  2. The counters beside the cells go 1, 2, 3, … from top to bottom.
  3. The numbers and charts match what you reported.

If a cell fails, that's good news: you found the hidden state before your reader did. Recreate whatever the failing cell needs in an earlier cell, then restart and run all again.

#Write the setup and the checks into the notebook

Restart-and-run-all proves the notebook runs. Two more habits help a reader trust what it ran on.

Record versions and parameters in the first cell. Library updates occasionally change defaults, so print what you used, and put every choice someone might want to change (seed, file name, cutoff values) in one place:

Your Colab output will show different version numbers; that's exactly why it's worth printing them.

Turn assumptions into assertions. An assert stops the notebook with a message if something you believed about the data stops being true:

Now suppose next month's file arrives with a typo: someone entered 4500 minutes instead of 45. The notebook refuses to continue, and points straight at the problem:

Without that line, the 4500 would quietly push the average up by about 1,500 minutes and land in a chart. An AssertionError at the top of the notebook is far better than a wrong number at the bottom.

#The shape of a reproducible notebook

Put all of this together and most analysis notebooks follow the same order. Each step only uses variables created in the steps before it:

Use text cells with headings for each section. Colab builds a clickable Table of contents in the left sidebar from those headings, so a reader can jump straight to the findings. And if a step happened outside the notebook (you fixed a typo in a spreadsheet, or filtered rows by clicking), it isn't reproducible. Move it into code.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Your notebook runs perfectly for you, but a teammate gets NameError: name 'clean' is not defined on Run all. What's the most likely cause?

  • A broken library gives an ImportError or AttributeError, not a missing variable name.

  • Your memory kept the old variable; a fresh runtime never creates it. Restart session and run all would have shown you the same error.

  • It isn't. Any variable name that was never assigned gives this error.

Show answer

B. Your memory kept the old variable; a fresh runtime never creates it. Restart session and run all would have shown you the same error.

2A cell contains df["price"] = df["price"] * 1.08 to add 8% tax. You run it three times while fixing a chart below it. What happened to the prices?

  • pandas has no idea what the column means. Each run multiplies the current values again.

  • 1.08 × 1.08 × 1.08 ≈ 1.26. Writing df["price_with_tax"] = df["price"] * 1.08 instead would be safe to rerun.

  • Reassigning a column is always allowed, which is exactly why the bug is silent.

Show answer

B. 1.08 × 1.08 × 1.08 ≈ 1.26. Writing df["price_with_tax"] = df["price"] * 1.08 instead would be safe to rerun.

3Seed 42 shows a big difference between two groups; seeds 1 through 10 show small or none. What should you report?

  • Reproducible doesn't mean representative. Picking the seed after seeing results misleads readers.

  • How much the result moves between seeds is part of the finding.

  • Random sampling is fine; you just have to report the variation honestly.

Show answer

B. How much the result moves between seeds is part of the finding.

Key takeaways

  • The runtime's memory, not the page, is what code actually uses. Deleted cells and out-of-order runs leave hidden state behind.
  • Never overwrite raw data. Derive new variables so every cell is safe to rerun.
  • Seed every random step, choose the seed up front, and report how much results vary.
  • Use Runtime › Restart session and run all before sharing anything.
  • Put versions, parameters, and assertions near the top so readers know what ran and what was checked.

#Further reading

  • Ten simple rules for writing and sharing computational analyses in Jupyter Notebooks (opens in a new tab): a short, practical paper from researchers who share notebooks for a living.
  • The Turing Way: Guide for Reproducible Research (opens in a new tab): a free community handbook on making any analysis reproducible, from data to environments.
  • NumPy random Generator (opens in a new tab): how default_rng and seeds work, and why it replaced the older np.random.seed.

What you'll learn

  • Put every adjustable choice in one parameters cell, using Colab form fields.
  • Clean data in code and keep a log of how many rows each step removed.
  • Pick one chart per question and keep colors consistent across all of them.
  • Combine the charts into a single dashboard figure and export it with predictable file names.
  • Generate an executive summary from computed values so it can never disagree with the data.

Last year, someone on the student council made a slick chart showing which school bus was late most often. It got the principal's attention. This year nobody can rebuild it: the spreadsheet had rows deleted by hand, a filter was clicked on and never noted, and the "late" cutoff isn't written down anywhere.

You're going to build the replacement, a notebook that goes from the raw arrival log to a finished report with one Run all. Here's the shape of what you'll produce:

#Step 1: A parameters cell at the top

Every choice that someone might reasonably question goes here: the seed, the definition of "late," the routes, and the file names. In Colab, the # @param comments turn into form fields beside the code, so a reader can change the late cutoff with a text box and rerun.

ROUTE_COLORS is a parameter too. Deciding once that Route 7 is orange means it's orange in every chart, and readers learn the code after the first one.

#Step 2: Get the raw file

In real life, the transportation office would email you bus_arrivals_raw.csv and you'd upload it to Colab's file panel. Here, a simulation writes one with the same problems real GPS logs have: some trips recorded twice, and a few impossible delays from GPS glitches. Treat this cell as "the office sent the file," and never edit the CSV by hand.

(Spoiler, since you can read the simulation: Route 7 got a new schedule on day 31, and Route 12's route floods when it rains. Your analysis should find both without being told.)

#Step 3: Clean in code, and log every step

Each cleaning step records how many rows it removed. That log goes into the report, so a reader can see exactly what happened to the data between the file and the charts.

The two assertions encode facts about buses: each route arrives once per school day, and only three routes exist. If next month's file breaks either one, the notebook stops here instead of drawing a confident chart from bad rows. Notice that the cleaning never touches raw; it builds clean from it, so rerunning the cell is always safe.

#Step 4: One summary table answers "which bus, and when?"

Three findings jump out: Route 7 is late most often overall but improved sharply partway through; Route 12 is fine on dry days and almost always late in the rain; Route 3 is reliable. Each finding is a different kind of question, so each gets a different chart.

#Step 5: One chart per question

Question Kind of question Chart
How spread out are each route's delays? Distribution Strip plot with medians
Did Route 7 get better? Change over time Line of weekly % late
Does rain matter, and for which route? Comparing amounts across groups Grouped bars, from zero

Rather than three separate figures, build them as functions that draw onto an axis you pass in. That way the same code can draw a chart on its own or as a panel of a dashboard.

The drawn chart is the weekly one, on its own. Look at how the titles are written: each states the finding, and the Route 7 numbers are filled in from before and after. In the weather chart, every bar is labeled "dry" or "rain" directly, so it doesn't rely on the lighter shade alone.

💡 Tip

Five trips per week makes the weekly line jumpy: one late bus moves a point by 20 percentage points. That's honest, but say so in the report, and don't read meaning into a single week's spike.

#Step 6: Assemble the dashboard and export it

A dashboard here is just one figure with several panels and a title that tells the reader what the whole thing means. The three functions draw onto three axes:

To export it from Colab, add these lines at the end of that same cell. Saving in the cell that draws the figure avoids saving a blank or half-finished one, and numbered, descriptive file names keep the report's figures in order:

PNG at dpi=200 stays sharp in slides and documents; SVG stays crisp at any size on web pages. files.download copies the file to your computer, and the saved files also appear in Colab's Files panel on the left.

#Step 7: Write the executive summary from the numbers

An executive summary is the paragraph a busy reader reads instead of everything else: the main findings, how big they are, and the main limits. Building it with f-strings means every number in it comes from the same variables as the charts, so the text can't drift out of sync with the data.

Try it: set LATE_AFTER_MIN = 3, choose Runtime › Run all, and every number in the summary, the chart titles, and the dashboard changes together. That's the whole point of the parameters cell. Note that the limits section is part of the summary, not a footnote. A reader who only reads this paragraph still learns what the data can't tell them.

#Step 8: Lock the published numbers

Once the report is shared, add one last cell that checks the headline numbers haven't changed. If someone edits a cleaning rule later and the numbers shift, this cell fails and tells them the published report no longer matches the notebook. (If you tried other cutoffs in Step 7, set LATE_AFTER_MIN back to 5 first.)

Then do the final test from the Notes: Runtime › Restart session and run all. The report should rebuild itself, end to end, with no errors and the same numbers.

#The finished notebook

Your finished notebook is Steps 1 to 8 in order, each under its own text-cell heading, so Colab's table of contents doubles as the report's outline:

Text-cell heading Code it holds
Question and setup Step 1: parameters, colors, versions
Raw data Step 2: load the file (never edited by hand)
Cleaning Step 3: cleaning log and assertions
Results Step 4: summary tables
Charts and dashboard Steps 5 and 6: drawing functions, dashboard, export
Executive summary Step 7: the generated summary
Checks Step 8: locked numbers

To prove the pipeline depends on nothing hidden, here is its core as one standalone cell. Paste it into a brand-new notebook and it reproduces the published headline numbers:

The random calls happen in exactly the same order as in Step 2, which is why the numbers match. If you reorder the loop (all of Route 3's days first, say), the seed produces different delays and the final assertion fails. With seeds, the order of random calls is part of the recipe.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the executive summary use f-strings like {before:.0f}% instead of typing "80%"?

  • Speed isn't the issue; a summary prints in an instant either way.

  • A typed "80%" stays 80% even after a cleaning rule changes. A computed one can't disagree with the analysis.

  • Text cells can hold any text. The risk is that typed numbers go stale.

Show answer

B. A typed "80%" stays 80% even after a cleaning rule changes. A computed one can't disagree with the analysis.

2Why are the three charts written as functions that take an ax argument?

  • draw_weekly(ax) doesn't care which axis it gets, so there's one version of each chart to keep correct.

  • You can draw directly with plt.plot. Functions just avoid copying code between the single charts and the dashboard.

  • Memory use is the same. The benefit is avoiding duplicate code.

Show answer

A. draw_weekly(ax) doesn't care which axis it gets, so there's one version of each chart to keep correct.

3A teammate changes VALID_DELAY to (-15, 60) and the "lock the published numbers" cell fails. What does that tell you?

  • The assertion did its job: it caught a change that affects published results.

  • That's the purpose of the check. Either revert the change, or update the report and say why the numbers moved.

  • Assertions run whenever their cell runs.

Show answer

B. That's the purpose of the check. Either revert the change, or update the report and say why the numbers moved.

Key takeaways

  • One parameters cell holds every choice a reader might question; Colab's # @param turns them into form fields.
  • Clean from raw into a new DataFrame, log rows removed at each step, and assert facts about the data.
  • Match each question to a chart type, keep one color per entity, and write titles that state findings.
  • Draw charts with functions that take an axis, then reuse them in a dashboard figure.
  • Export with savefig in the drawing cell, using numbered, descriptive file names.
  • Build the executive summary, including limits, from computed values, and lock the published numbers with assertions.
