What you'll learn

  • Add seeds to random steps and prove two runs match.
  • Reorder and repair cells so a notebook survives Restart session and run all.
  • Generate report text and chart titles from computed values.
  • Write data checks that report every problem at once.
  • Measure and report how much a sampled result varies.

Run the setup cell first. Every exercise uses these imports and colors.

#Warm-up

Which of these four cells could you run twice in a row and get the same result both times? Decide before reading the answer below.

B and D are safe: they compute something new from inputs they don't change. A adds 5 again on every run. C crashes on the second run with KeyError, because notes is already gone, which at least tells you something is wrong. A fails silently, and that makes it the worst of the four.

#Exercise 1: Make a sampled average repeatable

average_of_sample gives a different answer every time it's called. Add a seed parameter so the same seed always gives the same answer, and prove it with an assert. Then call it with seeds 0 to 49 and print the lowest and highest result next to the true average of all 2,000 rows.

Sample output: Seeds 0-49: lowest __, highest __, true average __.

Need a hint?

DataFrame.sample takes random_state=. Pass the seed through to it. A dictionary or list comprehension over range(50) collects the 50 results.

Show solution

The assertion proves repeatability, and the range shows that two perfectly reproducible analyses with different seeds can disagree by many minutes. A sample of 30 is small; reporting the range keeps readers from over-trusting any single run.

#Exercise 2: Survive Restart session and run all

Jamal's notebook worked all week. After a restart, Run all crashes at the second cell. Here are his cells in page order:

Explain why it worked before the restart, then fix the notebook so it runs top to bottom on a fresh runtime. Add an assert that would catch a negative payment.

Need a hint?

Jamal ran Cell 3 at some point last week, so club_total was already in memory when he edited Cell 2. Every cell may only use names created above it.

Show solution

Before the restart, club_total existed in memory from an earlier run of the calculation cell, so the print worked even though it sat above the line that creates club_total. Ordering the cells as data, then calculations, then report means each one only depends on cells above it.

#Exercise 3: Replace the hand-typed numbers

A reporter typed this summary last month. The data has since been updated.

Write a function fundraiser_summary(df) that builds the same three facts from the data, then print both versions. How many of the typed numbers are now wrong?

Need a hint?

df.loc[df["raised"].idxmax()] gives the top row. (df["raised"] >= df["goal"]).sum() counts goals met. Format money with f"${value:,}".

Show solution

All three facts changed: the top amount, the number of clubs that met their goal, and the total. Nobody would have noticed, because a typed sentence never complains when the data under it moves. The computed version updates on every run.

#Exercise 4: Report every data problem at once

An assert stops at the first failure, which means fixing problems one rerun at a time. Write a function check_survey(df) that runs all of these checks and returns a list of the ones that fail, so you see everything in one run:

  • student_id has no duplicates
  • grade is between 9 and 12
  • sleep_hours is between 0 and 16
  • no column has missing values

Sample output: one line per failed check, then a final assert that stops the notebook if the list isn't empty.

Need a hint?

Build a dictionary that maps each check's description to a True/False result, then keep the descriptions whose result is False. Comparisons with NaN are False, so test for missing values separately with .isna().

Show solution

Three checks fail: a duplicated ID, a grade of 13, and a missing sleep value. The printout lists all three before the AssertionError stops the notebook. Notice the sleep-hours check uses dropna() so a missing value is reported once, by the check designed for it, rather than also making the range check fail.

#Exercise 5: A titled chart and a predictable file name

Draw a bar chart of the fundraiser from Exercise 3 with bars from zero, a short black goal marker for each club, and a title computed from the data. Then write figure_filename(number, description) that turns (2, "Fundraiser: raised vs. goal!") into fig02_fundraiser_raised_vs_goal.png, and test it with assert.

Need a hint?

For the goal markers, ax.scatter(x, goals, marker="_", s=900) draws a wide horizontal tick. For the file name, lowercase the text, then re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "_", text).strip("_") replaces every run of other characters with one underscore.

Show solution

Two-digit numbering (fig02) keeps files in order when sorted by name, even past fig09. Blue bars mark clubs that met their goal; the black ticks carry the goals themselves, so the chart reads correctly in grayscale.

#Exercise 6: Generate an executive summary

Write executive_summary(question, findings, limits) where findings and limits are lists of strings. It should return text with the question on the first line, the findings as a numbered list, and the limits as a single sentence starting with "Limits:". Use it with findings computed from fundraiser.

Need a hint?

"\n".join(f"{i}. {text}" for i, text in enumerate(findings, start=1)) builds the numbered list. Join the limits with "; ".

Show solution

The function only handles layout; every number arrives already computed. Keeping the wording (your judgment) separate from the numbers (the data) means you can rewrite a sentence without risk of changing a figure.

#Challenge: How much does the answer depend on the seed?

A study team estimates the share of students who walk to school by surveying a random 60 of the school's 900 students. Write run_analysis(seed) that draws the sample with that seed and returns the walking share as a percent. Run it for seeds 0 to 199, draw a histogram of the 200 results with the true share marked, and print the range that holds the middle 95% of results.

Need a hint?

np.percentile(results, [2.5, 97.5]) gives the bounds of the middle 95%. Mark the truth with ax.axvline. A sample of 60 can only produce shares that are multiples of 1/60, so give each possible count its own bin; equal-width bins of a round size would make some bars look taller just because they cover two possible values.

Show solution

A single seed gives one number with false precision. The spread across seeds shows that with only 60 students, an honest report sounds like "about a third walk, give or take 12 points." This range is close to what a statistician would call a confidence interval, and you got it with nothing but a loop and a seed.

What you'll learn

  • Describe what the finished capstone includes and how it will be judged.
  • Pick a project idea and dataset that match your time and skills.
  • Rewrite a vague topic as a specific question with a comparison, a change, or a relationship.
  • Run a first look that tests whether a dataset can answer your question before you commit to it.
  • Fill in a planning template, including the biases you expect before you see results.

Every skill from this course comes together here: loading and cleaning data, summarizing it, choosing honest charts, questioning your own claims, and packaging it all in a notebook anyone can rerun. The finished product is a reproducible data investigation, the kind of analysis you could hand to a teacher, a club, or a future employer and have them get your exact results.

#What you'll hand in

A Google Colab notebook (shared as a link or downloaded as an .ipynb file) that:

  1. States one clear question at the top, with where the data came from and its license or terms.
  2. Runs from top to bottom with Runtime › Restart session and run all, with no errors.
  3. Loads the raw data without hand edits, cleans it in code, and logs what each cleaning step removed.
  4. Checks its own assumptions with assertions.
  5. Summarizes the data with appropriate centers and spreads.
  6. Includes at least three charts, each chosen for a different question, with titles that state findings.
  7. Discusses bias and limitations: who's in the data, who isn't, and what you can and can't conclude.
  8. Opens (or closes) with an executive summary whose numbers are computed, not typed.
  9. Exports its figures, and combines the key ones into a dashboard figure or a one-page report.

The last lesson of this module has the full rubric. You'll build in milestones, so no single sitting has to do everything.

#Five project ideas, from starter to stretch

Pick one, or adapt one to something you care about. Every option is free, and the first three need no download at all.

Level Project Data A good starting question
Starter Your own two-week log Track something about yourself daily: sleep, screen time, steps, practice minutes Do I sleep less on nights I use my phone after 10 p.m.?
Starter What makes a wine a wine sklearn.datasets.load_wine: 178 wines from three growers in one region of Italy Which chemical measurements differ most between the three growers?
Intermediate BMI and diabetes progression sklearn.datasets.load_diabetes(scaled=False): 442 patients from one medical study Is higher BMI linked to faster disease progression, and does it hold across age groups?
Intermediate Your city, in numbers A city or national open-data portal (such as data.gov (opens in a new tab)): service requests, bike-share trips, library checkouts Have pothole reports changed over the last three years, and in which neighborhoods?
Stretch Check a published chart A chart from the news plus its source data (for example from Our World in Data (opens in a new tab)) Does the chart's claim hold up when I rebuild it honestly and check for confounders?

A few cautions. If you log your own data, keep it to things you're comfortable sharing, and don't collect data about other people without their permission. For open-data portals, read the dataset's documentation page before anything else: it tells you what each column means, how the data was collected, and what you're allowed to do with it.

💡 Tip

The starter projects aren't "easier grades." A two-week log has only 14 rows, which makes the limitations section genuinely interesting: what can 14 nights about one person tell you, and what can't they?

#Turn a topic into a question

"Sleep" is a topic. "Screen time and sleep" is still a topic. A question you can answer has three parts: what you'll measure, what you'll compare (between groups, over time, or against another variable), and who or when it's about.

Vague Answerable
Wine chemistry Which three of the 13 measurements differ most between the three growers?
Is BMI bad? Among the 442 patients in this study, is BMI correlated with disease progression one year later, and does the link hold within age groups?
City potholes Did pothole reports per month rise or fall from 2023 to 2025, and was the change similar across neighborhoods?

Notice what the answerable versions avoid: "cause," "everyone," and "prove." Those words promise more than observational data can deliver, and Module 6 showed you why.

#Run a 15-minute first look

Before you commit to a dataset, spend fifteen minutes checking it can answer your question. Here's a first look at the wine data for the starter question above:

Four questions decide whether this dataset works. Is it big enough? 178 rows, roughly 50 to 70 per group: enough to compare groups, not enough for fine detail. Is it clean? No missing values, which is rare and worth noting. Does it have the columns I need? Yes, a group label and 13 measurements. Do the groups differ at all? One chart answers that:

That's a promising first look: grower 2's wines don't overlap grower 0's at all on this one measurement, while grower 1 sits in between and overlaps both. The question clearly has an answer worth finding, and it already hints that you'll need more than one measurement to tell grower 1 apart. If your first look shows a dataset is tiny, mostly empty, or missing the column your question needs, change the question or the dataset now, not after a week of work.

⚠️ Watch out

Reading the documentation late. The wine data's documentation says only that the wines come from one region of Italy and three growers. Nothing in the data tells you about wines from anywhere else, and a claim about "red wines" in general would go beyond it. Read the data's description before you write your question, so your question stays inside what the data covers.

#Write your plan

Copy this template into the first text cell of your capstone notebook and fill it in. Some answers will change as you work; update them, and keep the old versions in a "changes" note at the bottom so a reader can see how the plan evolved.

The bias pre-mortem is the most important part. Writing down possible problems before you see any results keeps you honest later: you can't quietly decide a confounder doesn't matter just because your finding is exciting.

#Milestones

Build in stages, and run Restart session and run all at the end of every one. A notebook that breaks at milestone 2 is easy to fix; one that breaks at milestone 6 with five milestones of hidden state behind it is not.

The next lesson walks through milestones 2 to 6 on a worked example with a starter notebook you can adapt. The one after covers milestone 7: testing, polishing, and presenting.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone is a notebook that reruns cleanly and turns raw data into an honest, well-charted answer to one question.
  • Pick a project for the question you care about; small datasets make for rich limitations sections.
  • An answerable question names a measurement, a comparison, and who or when.
  • A 15-minute first look tests size, cleanliness, columns, and whether groups differ before you commit.
  • Write the bias pre-mortem before you see results, and end every milestone with Restart session and run all.

  • scikit-learn toy datasets (opens in a new tab): the documentation for the wine and diabetes datasets, including where they came from.
  • Our World in Data (opens in a new tab): thousands of documented charts on health, energy, and the economy, each with a downloadable CSV and sources.
  • Kaggle Learn: Data Visualization (opens in a new tab): free short lessons to practice more chart types once your capstone is done.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Set up a capstone notebook from a skeleton with clear sections and a parameters cell.
  • Write a data dictionary, including what the documentation doesn't tell you.
  • Check a relationship for a confounder by comparing it within groups.
  • Build three charts that answer three different questions, and combine them into a dashboard.
  • Generate an executive summary whose limits are as specific as its findings.

This lesson builds one complete capstone, start to finish, so you can see every milestone done properly before doing it on your own data. The example is the intermediate project from the planning lesson:

Among the 442 patients in this study, is body mass index (BMI) linked to disease progression one year later, and does the link hold within age groups?

Each milestone ends with a Your turn box saying what to do in your own notebook. Work through a milestone here, do it for your project, then run Runtime › Restart session and run all before moving on.

#The starter skeleton

Create a new Colab notebook and paste this into the first code cell. Add a text cell above it with your project title, your question, and where the data came from. The files import lets you upload a CSV from your computer if your data isn't online.

Reading from a link is better than uploading: a teammate who opens your notebook gets the data automatically. If you must upload, say so in a text cell, and name the exact file.

#Milestone 2: Load, document, clean, and check

The diabetes data ships with scikit-learn, so there's nothing to upload. scaled=False gives the original units instead of the standardized values scikit-learn uses by default.

Before cleaning anything, write a data dictionary: one row per column you'll use, saying what it means and where that meaning came from. Here it comes from the scikit-learn documentation, which also reveals a gap:

Two gaps already: we don't know which sex code means what, and "progression" has no stated units. Neither stops the analysis, but both go in the limitations, and the sex codes stay as "group 1" and "group 2" in every chart. Guessing would put an invented fact into the report.

Now clean and check. This dataset is unusually tidy, so the cleaning log is short, but the checks still earn their place: they'd catch a wrong file or a future version with different units.

The BMI groups use the standard adult cut-offs of 25 and 30. The age groups are a choice made to give each group well over 100 patients; write choices like that down, because a reader might reasonably pick different ones.

📝 Note

Your turn. Load your data, write a data dictionary for every column you'll use (with a "gap" note wherever the documentation is silent), clean in code with a log, and add at least three assertions that describe facts about your data. Then restart and run all.

#Milestone 3: Summaries and distributions

Look at each key variable on its own before looking at relationships. The outcome first:

Progression is right-skewed: most patients cluster below 150, and a long tail stretches past 300. That's why the summaries below use medians. The ages run from 19 to 79, so this study says nothing about children or people over 79.

📝 Note

Your turn. Describe your key variables with describe() and a histogram each. Decide mean or median for each one, and write a sentence saying why.

#Milestone 4: The relationship, then the bias checks

The main question is about two numeric variables, so it's a scatter plot with r:

A correlation of 0.59 is moderately strong, and the scatter shows it's roughly a straight-line trend, not a curve r would misread. Now be your own skeptic. Older patients might have both higher BMI and faster progression, which would make age a confounder. So check whether the BMI link survives within each age group, and within each sex group:

The BMI link is about the same strength in every age group (r from 0.55 to 0.59), and it's clearly present in both sex groups (0.53 and 0.65). Age and BMI are only weakly related (r = 0.19), so age can't be what's producing the pattern. That's a real finding: the relationship isn't an artifact of the one confounder we can test.

What this check can't rule out is anything not in the data: diet, exercise, medication, income. And it's still correlation. Nothing here shows that changing a patient's BMI would change their progression.

📝 Note

Your turn. Make the chart that answers your main question. Then name at least one confounder you can test with your columns, and check whether your pattern holds within its groups. Write down the confounders you can't test, too.

#Milestone 5: Three charts and a dashboard

Each chart answers a different question, and the BMI groups keep the same colors throughout:

Chart Question it answers
Strip plot of progression by BMI group How different are the groups, and how much do they overlap?
Scatter of BMI and progression Is it a steady trend, and how strong?
Median progression by BMI group, within each age group Does the pattern hold at every age?

Notice the middle panel is gray, not a fourth color: it shows all patients, not a group, so it shouldn't borrow a group's color. To export, add the lines from the Module 7 build-along to the end of this cell, with your own file names:

📝 Note

Your turn. Build at least three charts for three different questions, with titles that state findings and colors that follow entities. Combine the key ones into one dashboard figure and export it.

#Milestone 6: Executive summary and limits

Everything in the summary comes from variables computed above. The limits are just as specific as the findings, which is what makes them useful.

A reader who stops after this paragraph knows the answer, how big it is, how sure to be, and what it doesn't cover.

📝 Note

Your turn. Write your executive summary as an f-string: the question, two to four numbered findings with computed numbers, and specific limits drawn from your bias pre-mortem and your data dictionary's gaps.

Key takeaways

  • Start from a skeleton with a parameters cell, and read data from a link when you can.
  • A data dictionary records meanings and their sources, including the gaps you must not fill with guesses.
  • Look at each variable alone before looking at relationships, and let skew decide between mean and median.
  • Test a relationship within groups of any confounder you have, and list the confounders you can't test.
  • Build each chart for one question, keep colors tied to entities, and compute every number in the summary.

#Further reading

  • scikit-learn load_diabetes (opens in a new tab): the loader's options, including scaled=False and as_frame=True.
  • Fundamentals of Data Visualization: titles, captions, and tables (opens in a new tab): how to write figure titles and captions that carry the message.
  • Matplotlib: arranging multiple Axes in a Figure (opens in a new tab): subplots, width_ratios, and other ways to lay out a dashboard.

What you'll learn

  • Run a test plan that proves your notebook reruns, catches bad data, and doesn't depend on arbitrary choices.
  • Scan your own summary for words that claim more than the data shows.
  • Polish a chart from default to presentation quality, with a checklist.
  • Structure a five-minute presentation or one-page report around your findings and limits.
  • Assess your capstone with the rubric and reflect on what you'd do next.

You present your findings, and the first question from the audience is: "If I run your notebook, will I get 0.59 too?" The second is: "What if you'd split the ages differently?" Good investigators have already asked themselves both. This lesson is the checklist that makes sure you have, and then it gets your work ready to show.

The examples continue the diabetes investigation from the previous lesson. Run this cell to rebuild its data:

#The test plan

# Test How Passes when
1 Fresh run Runtime › Restart session and run all No errors; cell counters go 1, 2, 3… in order
2 Someone else's run Share the notebook with Share (top right in Colab) and ask a friend to run all in their own account Their headline numbers match yours exactly
3 Tampered data Feed your checks a copy of the data with a planted error The checks catch it
4 Seeds If anything is random, change SEED and rerun The conclusions don't change (small numbers may)
5 Cutoffs Change one choice you made (a group boundary, a threshold) The main finding survives, or you report that it doesn't
6 Claims Read every sentence of your summary against your results Every claim points to a number or chart above it

Tests 1 and 2 are the reproducibility tests from Module 7, and test 2 is the one people skip. It catches the problems you can't see from your own account: a file only you uploaded, a Google Drive path only you can reach, a library only you installed.

#Test 3: Plant an error and see if your checks catch it

Assertions that never fire might be checking nothing. Put your checks in a function, then give it a copy of the data with mistakes planted in it:

Both planted errors were caught, each by the check meant for it (the range checks skip blanks with dropna(), so a missing value is reported only once). If one slipped through, you'd know a check was missing, and that's much better to learn now than after a slipped decimal ends up in your scatter plot.

#Test 5: Does the finding survive a different cutoff?

The age groups (under 40, 40 to 54, 55 and over) were a judgment call. Try other reasonable splits and see whether "the BMI link holds in every age group" stays true:

Every split gives a clearly positive r in every group, so the finding doesn't depend on where the lines were drawn. Say so in your report; it's one sentence and it answers the audience's second question before they ask it. If a different reasonable choice had flipped your finding, that would belong in your limitations, not in a drawer.

#Test 6: Scan the summary for overclaiming

Some words promise more than observational data can deliver. A tiny scanner won't judge your reasoning, but it will point you at sentences worth rereading:

The draft trips three flags; the revision trips none, and it also says more: the sample, the strength, and the open question. A flagged word isn't automatically wrong ("we can't say what causes this" is fine), which is why the scanner flags and you decide.

#Polish the charts

Default charts answer "what does the data look like?" Presentation charts answer "what should I notice?" Here's the same data both ways:

Before you export any figure, check it against this list:

  • Title states the finding, computed from the data.
  • Axes have labels and units (or say "units not given" when the source doesn't provide them).
  • Bars start at zero; lines and scatters use a range that matches meaningful change.
  • Colors follow entities and stay the same across every chart; nothing depends on color alone.
  • Direct labels where they help, a legend only where needed, no clutter like heavy borders or 3D.
  • Readable at presentation size: open the exported PNG at full screen and read the smallest text from across the room.
  • Alt text written for each figure, describing what it shows and the main pattern.

#Present it in five minutes

Whether you speak, make slides, or write a one-page report, use the same five parts in this order:

  1. The question and why it matters (two sentences).
  2. The data: where it came from, who and what it covers, and what you cleaned.
  3. Two or three findings, one chart each. Say the chart's title aloud; it's your topic sentence.
  4. Limits: who isn't in the data, the confounders you couldn't test, and what you can't claim.
  5. What you'd do next with more time or better data.

Lead with the answer, not the process: "BMI and progression rise together at every age" beats "First I loaded the data." Keep your notebook open in another tab. When someone asks "how do you know it isn't just age?", you can show them the within-group check, which is the most convincing answer there is.

#The rubric

Criterion Excellent (4) Developing (2–3) Beginning (1)
Question and data Specific question; source, license, coverage, and a data dictionary with gaps noted Clear question; source named but coverage or dictionary thin Vague topic; source unclear
Reproducibility Restart session and run all passes, and a second person got the same numbers; parameters and seeds in one setup cell Runs top to bottom for the author; some hard-coded choices scattered through Errors on a fresh run, or depends on hand-edited files
Cleaning and checks Every step in code with a log; assertions that catch planted errors Cleaning in code, few checks Cleaning by hand or undocumented
Summaries Center and spread chosen for each variable's shape, with reasons Correct summaries, little explanation Means everywhere, regardless of skew or outliers
Charts At least three charts for three questions; honest axes; finding titles; consistent, accessible colors; dashboard exported Appropriate charts with some default titles or styling issues Charts that don't fit the question, or that mislead
Bias and limits Pre-mortem done early; confounder tested within groups; sample limits and untestable confounders named; sensitivity checked Limits listed but general ("more data needed") No discussion of bias or limits
Communication Computed executive summary; claims match the evidence; clear five-part presentation Summary present but with typed numbers or some overclaiming Findings hard to locate, or claims beyond the data

A strong capstone scores 4 on most rows. A project with modest findings and an excellent bias section can outscore one with a dramatic finding and no limits; that's on purpose.

#Reflect

Write short answers in a final text cell of your notebook:

  • What surprised you most in your data, and which chart showed it?
  • Which limitation would you most like to fix, and what data would fix it?
  • Where did your plan change, and why?
  • If someone repeated your analysis next year with new data, which assertion is most likely to fail first?

#Where to go next

  • Find more data to practice on. Tidy Tuesday (opens in a new tab) posts a new, documented dataset every week; the community started in R, but every dataset is a plain CSV that pandas reads directly.
  • Learn to predict, not just describe. The C4T machine learning courses build directly on the pandas, charts, and careful claims from this course.
  • Keep practicing charts. Kaggle Learn (opens in a new tab) has free short courses on pandas, visualization, and data cleaning with in-browser notebooks.
  • Publish your capstone. A notebook that reruns cleanly, with an honest limitations section, is a stronger portfolio piece than a flashy dashboard nobody can rebuild.

Key takeaways

  • Test that the notebook reruns for you and for someone else, and that its checks catch planted errors.
  • Change the choices you made (seeds, cutoffs) and report whether the findings survive.
  • Scan summaries for overclaiming words, then decide for yourself which ones are justified.
  • Polish charts with a checklist: finding titles, labels and units, honest axes, consistent colors, alt text.
  • Present in five parts, lead with the answer, and use your bias checks to answer the hardest questions.
